title_r: The effect of job stress and social interactions on nursing job performance : a replication study
abstract_r: Nursing has been described as one of the most stressful professions. This stress can affect many aspects of a nurse’s life such as physical health and emotional well-being which may contribute to professional burnout and job performance. In particular, job performance has been noted to have a curvilinear relationship to job stress (AbuAlRub, 2004). In addition, it has been found that social support is an effective coping mechanism to decrease job stress (AbuAlRub, 2004). This replication study will describe the correlation of job-related stress on the job performance of hospital nurses, as well as the effect of co-workers’ social support on the stress-performance relationship. Lazarus' Transactional Model of Stress and Coping is the theoretical framework. A convenience sample of registered nurses employed in direct patient care in hospitals throughout the state of Idaho will be utilized. The instruments utilized will be the Nursing Stress Scale, the Schwirian Six Dimension Scale of Nursing Performance and the McCain and Marklin Social Integration Scale. Demographics will also be collected from the study participants. Permission will be obtained from Ball State University. Findings will provide nursing leaders with information regarding the development of stress management strategies and the affect on the job performance of nurses.

title_r: The Categorical Information Quality Framework (CIQF): A Critical Assessment and Replication Study
abstract_r: The CIQF has been used widely by researchers and practitioners for several years. In this paper we have identified a number of methodological issues in the process used to create the framework, in particular the predominant use of graduate students in data collection, the sample size for the statistical analysis techniques used, researcher bias in the four groupings of information quality dimensions initially proposed, the use of descriptive statistics to test the proposed categories and the domain specificity of the framework. We propose a replication study that addresses these issues, using practitioners as subjects, a larger sample size to ensure a stable factor structure, factor analysis techniques to determine both the information quality dimension and the categories within the framework. The framework developed in our replication study will provide researchers with an empirically based and fully validated framework for future information quality research and practitioners with a sound basis for developing information quality metrics and information quality improvement

title_r: Comparative Stability of Cloned and Non-cloned Code: A Replication Study
abstract_r: Code cloning is an important software engineering aspect. It is a common software reuse principle that consists of duplicating source code within a program or across different systems owned or maintained by the same entity. There are several contradictory claims concerning the impact of cloning on software stability and maintenance effort. Some papers state that cloning is desired since it speeds up the development process and helps stakeholders meet the tight schedule and deliver on time. Other papers argue that code clone leads to code bloat and causes increase software maintenance costs due to copied defects and dead code. In this paper, we are replicating a previous study done on cloning by the original author. We are repeating his work using the same methods and metrics but with different subjects and experimenters. The paper we are addressing evaluates the impact of code cloning on code stability using three different stability-measuring methods. Our team will apply the same stability measurement techniques on a different software system developed in C programming language to determine generalizability, assure that the results are reliable, validate their outcomes, and to inspire new search by combining previous findings from related studies.

title_r: Motivational Anger Management Training: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication of Veenstra, Schneider, & Koole (2017) With a Virtual Reality-Based Serious Game
abstract_r: Recent findings indicate that letting people with chronic anger management problems make avoidance movements towards angry faces with a joystick lowers anger and aggression among this group (Veenstra, Schneider, & Koole, 2017). In the proposed study, we seek to conceptually replicate these findings. The proposed design is modelled after Study 2 of Veenstra, Schneider, and Koole (2017). Instead of joystick movements, however, we will manipulate whole body movements in a Virtual Reality (VR) environment among 78 undergraduate students. Participants with varying levels of trait anger will be randomly allocated to an experimental or control condition. In the experimental condition, participants will be instructed to lean backwards in response to avatars with angry facial expressions and to lean forward towards avatars with happy facial expressions. In the control condition, participants will receive the same instruction for happy-looking avatars, but not for angry-looking avatars, who will not appear in the VR environment. We predict that the experimental training will reduce anger and aggressive impulses among participants high (rather than low) in trait anger. The proposed study will provide a further test of embodied motivational models of anger management and fosters the development of VR-techniques that complements traditional cognitively based interventions.

title_r: Testing the Replicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior: A Large-Scale Multi-Sample Registered Replication Study
abstract_r: Identifying the determinants of social behavior, and the specific processes by which the determinants relate to behavior, are important in the development of theory to predict social behavior. Predicting behavior also has utility for organizations and stakeholders interested in developing effective interventions and strategies to promote behavior change. The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) is a prominent social psychological theory developed to predict social behavior. The theory derives its assumptions from theories of attitude and social cognition (Albarracín & Johnson, 2019; Eagly & Chaiken, 1993; Fishbein, 1967), and focuses on predicting intentional behavior from sets of beliefs about future behavioral engagement. The theory has been tested in over 2000 studies, and over 30 meta-analytic syntheses. Cumulative findings indicate its efficacy in accounting for variance in behaviors across multiple domains. However, considerable unresolved heterogeneity in effects has been observed, which could be attributable to methodological artifacts or genuine variability across contexts, behaviors, and populations. In addition, some theory predictions, particularly interactions among constructs, have not been tested and replicated consistently. The current project will conduct a large-scale replication of the theory in general population and student samples adopting an identical protocol and measures. The result of the study will be a series of data sets testing theory predictions analyzed by meta-analytic structural equation modeling.

title_r: Conceptual replication of "Mental fatigue impairs physical performance in humans"
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

In this replication study, we aim to replicate the main results of Marcora’s study, i.e., the effect of the demanding cognitive task on mental fatigue and exercise performance. The method section provides the details of the proposed design and data analysis.

summary: Conceptual replication of the following study:
Marcora, S. M., Staiano, W., & Manning, V. (2009). Mental fatigue impairs physical performance in humans. Journal of Applied Physiology, 106(3), 857–864. https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.91324.2008
Holgado D., Troya, E., Perales, JC. Vadillo, Ma. Sanabria, D.
Short introduction
Mental fatigue has been defined as a complex psychobiological state characterized by a prolonged period of demanding cognitive activity which normally impairs cognitive function [1]. Mental fatigue can be experienced physiologically, subjectively and behaviourally [2]. Altered parasympathetic activity [3] and brain activity [4], lack of energy [5] and decreased accuracy response [6], among others, are some of the consequences of mental fatigue. In the context of mental fatigue, it has been proposed that performing a long cognitive task would cause a depletion of internal resources impairing subsequent performance in a task which use similar resources. This is known as the “ego-depletion” effect, which has been widely studied in psychology, but has been questioned on numerous occasions [7,8]. 
Similar to the ego-depletion effect, in Sports science the effect of performing a long and challenging cognitive task before a physical exercise has attracted the interest of researchers. In a first experiment, Marcora et al. [9] sought to demonstrate that performing a long cognitive task before an exercise bout would impair physical performance, due to mental fatigue. In this experiment, participants completed a demanding cognitive task (mental fatigue condition) or watched a neutral documentary (control condition) for 90 minutes before a cycling time-to-exhaustion test at 80% of their peak power output. In the mental fatigue condition, participants completed a AX-continuous performance test (AX-CPT) to induce mental fatigue, as this task requires sustained attention, working memory, response inhibition, and error monitoring. The results of the study showed that in the mental fatigue condition participants were exhausted sooner than in the control condition. However, motivation or rate of perceived exertion (RPE) were not modified following the mental fatigue state. 
Given the doubts about the reliability of the ego-depletion effect, we believe that it is important to try to replicate this experiment  Second, upon a closer inspection of a recent review (cf. Pageaux and Lepers [10]), almost 50 percent of the studies showed no effects of mental fatigue on exercise performance variables. Third, most of the studies in this literature have a low sample size (mean n = 12, with an 8-22 range), which suggests that most published studies are underpowered to detect small but non-trivial effect sizes. Therefore, in this replication study, we aim to replicate the main results of Marcora’s study, i.e., the effect of the demanding cognitive task on mental fatigue and exercise performance. The method section provides the details of the proposed design and data analysis. 
Method
Design
The experiment will rely on a randomized, single-blind, counterbalanced, within-participant procedure design. This study has been approved by the University of Granada Ethics Committee (287/CEIH/2017). All experimental procedures comply with the Declaration of Helsinki. Before being recruited to the study, participants will read and sign the informed consent. All data will be entered in a case report form and subsequently in a computerized database. Participants will be naïve to the aim of the study in order to avoid expectation effects. Once they complete their participation, they will be debriefed with the purpose of the study.
Participants
Participants will be recruited from the student population of the Granada area, in Spain. Experimental sessions will take place in the Mind, Brain, Behaviour Research Centre, in the University of Granada, Spain. We will recruit male and females involved in regular aerobic training between 18 to 44 years, free of any known disease, and not taking any medication with the exception of contraceptives. Exclusion criteria will be the presence of symptomatic cardiomyopathy, metabolic disorders such as obesity (BMI >30) or diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, epilepsy, therapy with b-blockers and medications that would alter cardiovascular function, hormonal therapy, smoking, and neurological disorders.
Apparatus and materials
We will use a ViaSprint 150P cycle ergometer (Ergoline GmbH, Germany) to induce physical effort and to obtain power values, and a JAEGER Master Screen gas analyser (CareFusion GmbH, Germany) to provide a measure of gas exchange during the effort test. We will use a V800 Polar monitor (Polar Electro, Finland) to monitor and record (through a Polar H7 sensor band attached to the participant’s chest) the heart rate (HR) of the participants during the experiments. We will use a PC and the E-Prime software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) to control the stimulus presentation and response collection for the AX-CPT task. Moreover, we will use the same PC screen to reproduce the documentary in the control condition.
Procedure
Screening visit
During the first visit, participants will perform an incremental exercise test until exhaustion. The test will begin with a load of 50W for 2 minutes and the load will increment automatically in steep of 50 W every 2 minutes until volitional exhaustion (i.e. a pedal frequency of less than 60 rpm for more than 5 seconds despite strong verbal encouragement). Before the incremental exercise test, the position on the cycle ergometer will be adjusted for each participant and it will be recorded for the subsequent visits. We will use the 80% of the peak power output to establish the intensity of the time-to-exhaustion test. This value will be determined by the last steep completed or the fraction of the remaining time to complete that steep. 
Experimental session
After the familiarization visit, participants will attend to the lab in two separate visits to perform either the AX-CPT task or watch the documentary before the cycling time-to-exhaustion test. Upon arrival to the lab, participants will fill in the Brunel Mood Scale to assess mood (see Methods). After that, they will complete the treatment (see Methods). Once the task is completed, participants will fill in the psychological questionnaires and they will be positioned on the cycle ergometer to start the time-to-exhaustion test 15 min after the end of treatment. This constant-power cycling test is able to detect changes in endurance performance [11]. The time-to exhaustion cycling test will consist of a 3-min warm-up at 40% of peak power output followed by a rectangular workload corresponding to 80% of peak power output achieved in the screening visit. The test will finish when the pedal frequency is less than 60 RPM for more than 5 s despite standardized verbal encouragement. To increase participants’ motivation, we will offer a prize of 50€ for the best cycling performance after each treatment. The third visit will be exactly the same except for the treatment, which will be the opposite of the second visit.
AX-CPT task
In the mental fatigue condition, participants will complete during 90 minutes the AX-CPT task as stated in Marcora et al study [9]. In the AX-CPT [6], sequences of letters will be visually presented one at a time in a continuous fashion on a PC screen. Participants will seat in a room in front of 21’ PC screen. They will be instructed to press the right button on target trials and the left button otherwise (button responses will be reversed for left-handed people). Target trials will be defined as a cue-probe sequence in which the letter A appear as the cue and the letter X appear as the probe. The remaining letters of the alphabet served as invalid cues and nontarget probes, with the exception of the letters K and Y, which will be excluded because of their similarity in appearance to the letter X. Letter sequences will be presented in pseudorandom order, such that target (AX) trials occurred with 70% frequency and nontarget trials occurred with 30% frequency. Non-targets will be divided evenly (10% each) among the following trial types: BX trials, in which an invalid cue (i.e., non-A) preceded the target; AY trials, in which a valid cue will follow by a non-target probe (i.e., non-X); and BY trials, in which an invalid cue will follow by a non-target probe. To increase task difficulty, two white distractor letters (which could be any letter but A, K, X, or Y) will be presented between the cue and probe, which will be both red. All letters will be presented centrally, on a black background, for a duration of 300 ms in 24-point uppercase Courier font. Each letter will be followed by a 1,200-ms interval, which gives a 4,500-ms delay between the presentation of cue and probe stimuli. Any missed or incorrect response will elicit a bleep sound from two speakers as a prompt to increase speed and accuracy. To further increase engagement in the AX-CPT, a 50€ prize will be given for the best performance. Feedback on performance will be presented on the computer screen every 30 min as a percentage of the maximum possible score. Performance will be scored automatically by the computer on the basis of correct responses and response time. Because a reduction in vigilance and working memory are well-established effects of mental fatigue, the proportion of correct responses to the AX trials during the first and last 15-min period of the AX-CPT will be compared as manipulation check.
Control treatment
In the control condition, participants will watch two documentaries, which are able to maintain a neutral mood, during 90 minutes in the same PC screen used for the AX-CPT. These two documentaries will be the same (Spanish version) as those used by Marcora et al.: “World Class Trains—The Venice Simplon Orient Express” (Pegasus-Eagle Rock Entertainment, 2004) and “The History of Ferrari—The Definitive Story” (Boulevard Entertainment, 2006).
Psychological questionnaires
BRUMS. We will assess participants’ mood before and after the treatments by mean of the Brunel Mood Scale (BRUMS) developed by Terry et al. [12]. The questionnaire is based on Profile of Mood States, but it only contains 24 items (e.g., angry, uncertain, miserable, tired, nervous, energetic) divided into six respective subscales: anger, confusion, depression, fatigue, tension, and vigour. The items are answered on a 5-point Likert scale (0 not at all, 1 a little, 2 moderately, 3 quite a bit, 4 extremely), and each subscale, with four relevant items, can achieve a raw score in the range of 0 to 16. As stated by Marcora et al, the subscales of fatigue and vigour will be the main items to assess the state of mental fatigue.
Motivation. We will assess motivation after the treatment related to the time-to-exhaustion tests with the success motivation and intrinsic motivation scales developed and validated by Matthews et al. [13]. Each scale consists of 7 items (e.g., “I want to succeed on the task” and “I am concerned about not doing as well as I can”) scored on a 5-point Likert scale (0 not at all, 1 a little bit, 2 somewhat, 3 very much, 4 extremely). The final score of the questionnaire will range between 0 and 28.
Planned sample size
The sample size will be determined following a Bayesian approach. We plan to collect data from a minimum of 30 participants. Then, we will monitor the Bayes factor (for the average time in the time-to-exhaustion test) and stop the experiment whenever the Bayes factor reaches moderate evidence to either support (BF > 6) or to reject the null hypothesis (BF < 1/6). Even if none of these thresholds is reached, we will terminate data collection if the sample size reaches 50 participants or if none of the previous criteria is met by June 16th, 2019.
Statistical analysis
Specifically, we plan to calculate the default Bayes factor for an paired, one-sided t-test (mental fatigue vs control) using the open-source JASP statistical package. We will use a one-sided Bayesian test of the null hypothesis against the alternative hypothesis that the mental fatigue induced by AX-CPT task would impair the subsequent exercise performance with respect to the control condition, modelled with a Cauchy prior scaled at 0.7. If data from the time-to-exhaustion test do not follow a normal distribution, we will use a one-sided non-parametric Bayesian test.
The dependant variables for the time-to-exhaustion test will be the average time completed by the participants, the average heart rate and the session RPE. 
Manipulation check
The psychological variables for the mental fatigue or control condition will be the BRUMS values for fatigue and vigour, and the upcoming motivation to performance physical task.
We will use the VAS to check the task demands of mental fatigue and control condition to the following questions: 1) What is your activation level now?” 2) “What is your physical fatigue level now?” and 3) “What is your mental fatigue level now?”. It will be analysed by (normalized) rating change: post-test rating minus pre-test rating divided by post-test ratting plus pre-test rating. 
Data collection
Data collection will begin on March 12th, 2019.

title_r: Does cognitive inflexibility predict violent extremist behaviour intentions? A registered direct replication report of Zmigrod, Rentfrow, & Robbins, 2019
abstract_r: Purpose Research assessing violent extremist risk factors thus far largely ignored the role of cognitive processes. Zmigrod and colleagues (2019a) addressed this gap and presented first systematic evidence that lower levels of cognitive flexibility predict a higher willingness to fight and, ultimately, die for a national ingroup. This finding has important theoretical and practical implications. In order to strengthen the potential contribution of Zmigrod et al.’s work, we will conduct a registered direct replication of Study 1. Extending the original study, we further examine whether the documented relationship still holds when a self‐report measure for cognitive flexibility is introduced and when analyses control for identity fusion. We also investigate if cognitive inflexibility solely predicts violent or also normative pro‐group behaviour intentions. Methods Following Zmigrod, Rentfrow, and Robbins (2019a), we will administer a cross‐sectional survey study. Participants ( N = 1,378) report their willingness to fight, die, and sacrifice themselves for the ingroup and complete the Remote Associates as well as Wisconsin Card Sorting tests. Afterwards, additional measures of self‐reported cognitive flexibility, identity fusion, and normative pro‐group behaviour are assessed. Results To be completed. Conclusions To be completed.

title_r: Does generation benefit learning for narrative and expository texts? A direct replication attempt
abstract_r: Abstract Generated information is better recognized and recalled than information that is read. This so‐called generation effect has been replicated several times for different types of material, including texts. Perhaps the most influential demonstration was by McDaniel et al. (1986, Journal of Memory and Language , 25 , 645–656; henceforth MEDC). This group tested whether the generation effect occurs only if the generation task stimulates cognitive processes not already stimulated by the text. Numerous studies, however, report difficulties replicating this text by generation‐task interaction, which suggests that the effect might only be found under conditions closer to the original method of MEDC. To test this assumption, we will closely replicate MEDC's Experiment 2 in German and English‐speaking samples. Replicating the effect would suggest that it can be reproduced, at least under limited conditions, which will provide the necessary foundation for future investigations into the boundary conditions of this effect, with an eye towards its utility in applied contexts.

title_r: A Multi-Lab Registered Replication and Extension of IJzerman et al. (2012): Social exclusion leads to lower peripheral temperatures
abstract_r: The authors replicated a study by IJzerman et al. (2012), which concluded that the experimental condition of social exclusion (vs. inclusion) in the Cyberball computer game decreases peripheral index finger temperature, but did so with a sample size smaller than the authors calculated was needed for their minimum effect size of interest (N=41 in the original; N=95 would be enough to replicate the effect with over 95% power even if it is 15% smaller than the original effect), in a single lab in a colder country (the Netherlands), yet concluded generalizability. The study received considerable news coverage (e.g., in the New York Times) and is well-cited (223 at the time of writing). The authors seek to overcome the limitations of the previous study by conducting a highly-powered replication of the effect (projected minimum N=500) in 8 different countries in 3 different climatic regions (Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia, France, Turkey, Singapore, Nigeria, and Poland). The authors also extended the study by measuring body parts other than the index finger (pinky finger, supraclavicular, and wrist) and measured a selection of questionnaires that have been shown to be of relevance for social thermoregulatory mechanisms. Given the considerable power of the study and the inclusion of different climatic regions, these extensions can advance theory on social thermoregulation in various important ways.

title_r: Does the motor system functionally contribute to keeping words in working memory? A pre-registered replication of Shebani and Pulvermüller (2013, Cortex)
abstract_r: Increasing evidence implicates the sensorimotor systems with high-level cognition, but the extent to which these systems play a functional role remains debated. Using an elegant design, Shebani and Pulvermüller (2013) reported that carrying out a demanding rhythmic task with the hands led to selective impairment of working memory for hand-related words (e.g., clap), while carrying out the same task with the feet led to selective memory impairment for foot-related words (e.g., kick). This striking double dissociation constitutes strong evidence for an embodied account of working memory, a system that has received scarce attention in the embodiment literature. However, the original study was likely underpowered and used suboptimal statistical analyses, raising questions about the robustness of the results. In fact, our Bayesian reanalysis with a more appropriate model yields inconclusive evidence for the effect (BF10 = 1.7). To re-examine this seminal finding, we here attempt an appropriately powered, fully pre-registered replication of the original study, following a sequential design with a maximal participant sample size over seven times that of the original (108 vs. 15). We will analyse the results with Bayesian generalized mixed models and use Bayes factors to quantify the evidence in support of the effect predicted by theories of embodied cognition.

title_r: Crosslinguistic influence and L2 grammar learning: Close replications of Ellis &amp; Sagarra (2011) and Tolentino &amp; Tokowicz (2014)
abstract_r: Investigations of crosslinguistic effects in SLA have contributed rich understandings about the ways in which prior language knowledge and experience can influence additional language learning. Building on this work, one recent line of research has examined the extent to which SLA findings about crosslinguistic influence can be used to improve L2 learning, indicating that explicit instruction tailored to address the nature of the crosslinguistic learning problem can improve L2 learning. At the same time, however, this line of inquiry is relatively novel and under-researched. The aim of this paper, therefore, is to suggest further research which might advance knowledge and understanding about the ways in which explicit instruction can facilitate L2 learning of crosslinguistically difficult target features. To this end, I lay the ground for a series of replications designed to understand the role of prior language knowledge and experience in L2 learning: Ellis and Sagarra (2011) and Tolentino and Tokowicz (2014). These studies were selected because they are grounded in empirical SLA research and SLA theory. In addition, these studies facilitate replication because they have either (i) made their data collection materials available in digital repositories or (ii) have robustly described their design and provided the stimuli used.

title_r: Revisiting the Moral Forecasting Error – A Preregistered Replication and Extension of “Are We More Moral Than We Think?”
abstract_r: Predictions about the future are often inaccurate, but the direction of prediction errors may vary. Contrary to research on the intention-behavior gap, where people fail to live up to their future ambitions, a study on “moral forecasting” found that people behaved more honestly than they predicted. Since this interesting prediction error has only been identified in a few studies and the direction of the effect may seem surprising, psychological science could benefit from a high-powered replication. In Experiment 1, we will conduct a close replication using the original cheating task and a general population sample from the same country as the original study (Canada). By extension, we will also include the “mind-game paradigm” as an established deception-free cheating task from behavioral economics, to assess task generalizability. If the primary hypothesis is supported, then we propose a second extension in Experiment 2, by examining whether a cognitive debiasing intervention can reduce the moral forecasting error in a general population sample from the US. As a final extension we will also examine the social dimension of lay beliefs, by assessing whether moral forecasts for other people exhibit the same prediction error as moral forecasts for oneself. In the current experiments, the planned sample size will provide 90% power to detect ¼ of the observed effect size from the original study.

title_r: Fear, Anxiety, and the Error-Related Negativity: A Registered Report of a Multi-Site Replication Study
abstract_r: The error-related negativity (ERN), a scalp-recorded neural index of error monitoring, was directly linked to anxiety in a highly influential paper by Hajcak et al. (2003), which found that individuals high in worry symptoms of anxiety show greater ERN amplitude than those low in worry. This research sparked a flurry of further investigations, with subsequent work proposing the ERN to be a putative neural marker for anxiety. However, almost two decades later, the robustness of the relationship between the ERN amplitude and anxiety has been called into question. As part of the #EEGManyLabs international collaborative (Pavlov et al., 2021), the proposed replication involves the collection of data from three highly-powered samples (n = 234 each) across nine collaborating sites in Germany, Norway, The Netherlands, Poland, Russia, and the United States. Participants for the replication will be selected from a larger pool and assigned to the following three groups based on their scores on worry and phobia symptom scales: 1) high worry group, 2) high phobia/low worry group, and 3) low worry/phobia (control) group, with 70-80 participants in each group. All three groups of participants will complete a modified color-word Stroop task, consistent with procedures of Hajcak et al. (2003), while EEG recordings are made. As per Hajcak et al. (2003), we expect a significant main effect of group, with a larger overall ERN in the worry group than in the phobia and control groups, suggesting that enhanced sensitivity to errors is specific to worry vs. phobia. In addition to individual analyses conducted within each replicating lab, we will pool data across study sites and fit a two-stage individual participant data meta-analysis. Replication of this study will help in further characterizing the ERN signal and its link to clinical phenomena.

title_r: A Proposal to Study Shoulder-Surfing Resistant Authentication for Augmented and Virtual Reality: Replication Study in the US
abstract_r: In recent years, augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR) technologies have advanced significantly, becoming more accessible and practical for various industries and applications. However, new digital threats have emerged as AR/VR usage increases such as data exchange in shared spaces. Prior research on graphical authentication has proposed the Things scheme [21] and we plan to adapt this in the AR/VR domain. The scheme in combination with the private display available to users in AR/VR is resistant to shoulder-surfing attacks. Inspired by the work of Duezguen et al. [12], who conducted a user study applying the Things scheme in AR with 16 users in Germany, this short paper proposes a replication study that will implement the Things scheme in both AR and VR. We will recruit eligible participants for the in-lab study which will involve the use of HoloLens and Valve Index to test the Things scheme and we will evaluate the effectiveness of the scheme, the interaction modes for usability, and users’ risk perception concerning security. Additionally, we will conduct a comparative analysis of cross-cultural disparities between the participants in Germany and in the USA.

title_r: Assessing visuospatial biases (pseudoneglect) using pupillometry: A replication and extension of Strauch et al. (2022)
abstract_r: Strauch et al. (2022) introduced a novel approach to assess biases of visual attention, by measuring pupillary constriction in response to split-field stimuli, in which a bright patch is presented to one visual field and a dark patch to the other. Their study suggested that pupillary constriction is more pronounced in response to bright stimuli in the left visual field compared to the right, consistent with a neurotypical attentional bias towards the left side (pseudoneglect). This pupillometric bias was also found to correlate with performance on the greyscales task, an established behavioural measure of pseudoneglect. The present study seeks to replicate these findings, and investigates the influence of the eye of recording on the pupillary constriction bias measured by this split-field method.

title_r: Dementia mindset of caregivers providing residential care for older persons: study protocol for a replication study on the validation of the Dementia Mindset Scale
abstract_r: INTRODUCTION: Professional caregivers' perspectives on dementia and on people living with dementia (PlwD) can influence their feelings, judgements and behaviours in work situations, for example, how they think about symptoms, disease progression and the impact on a person's quality of life. Their individual dementia mindset, which can be investigated with the 12-item Dementia Mindset Scale (DMS), might influence job satisfaction, work-related well-being and person-centred care. The aim of the proposed replication study is to confirm the results of the original study of the DMS and to test whether a malleable mindset is correlated with higher levels of caregiver education, dementia-specific professional experience/competence and dementia knowledge. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: Professional caregivers in residential care facilities for older persons who work directly with PlwD will be asked to answer an anonymous web-based online survey. The survey encompasses five standardised questionnaires: the DMS, the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale, the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, the Job-related Affective Well-being Scale and the Sense of Competence in Dementia Care Staff Scale. In addition, job satisfaction, the educational background, professional experience and work situation are surveyed. For replication, the analyses will re-evaluate the psychometric properties (structural validity, model fit, internal consistency and predictive validity) by applying descriptive statistics, regression analysis, confirmatory factor analysis and correlation analysis. The additional analyses will use descriptive statistics, regression analysis and correlation analysis. Rasch analysis will be used to rank the difficulty of the items. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study was approved by the ethics committee of the German Society of Nursing Science (ID number 23-004). No personal information will be gathered. The results of the study will be distributed nationally and internationally through peer-reviewed academic journals, conferences, institutional websites and journals for nursing care practice.

title_r: Reversal or no reversal, that is the question – A conceptual replication of cross-cultural spatial-numerical associations
abstract_r: Reading direction is a central determinant of spatial–numerical associations, yet evidence from right-to-left (RL) readers remains inconsistent, ranging from weakened to reversed spatial-numerical associations (SNAs). Shaki et al. (2009) provided the only systematic cross-cultural comparison controlling for reading direction of both words and digits. They reported canonical SNAs in Canadian left-to-right (LR) readers, no SNAs in Hebrew readers with mixed habits (RL words, LR digits), and a reversed SNAs in Palestinian adults with consistent RL reading. Subsequent studies produced mixed results for populations with similar reading profiles, potentially reflecting uncontrolled bilingualism, differing directional habits, and culturally shaped spatial routines, such as object counting and finger counting. Given the theoretical importance of a reverse SNAs and the absence of a successful replication of this finding in standard parity tasks, the present study replicates Shaki et al. (2009), using the refined go/no-go methodology while additionally documenting participants’ object- and finger-counting preferences. We will test German LR readers, Israeli mixed-direction readers, and Palestinian RL readers with adequately powered samples (n = 39 per subgroup). This replication will clarify whether and how culturally transmitted directional habits contribute to spatial–numerical mappings.

title_r: A Replication Study of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-Induced Heart-Brain Coupling
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is a prominent stimulation target for the treatment of Major Depressive disorder (MDD) with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). The therapeutic effect of DLPFC stimulation likely stems from the DLPFC–subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) connectivity. A recent study suggested that there is an overlap of the hubs in the depression network, including the DLPFC, sgACC, and vagus nerve (VN), with the heart-brain axis, and that stimulation of these hubs consequently leads to heart rate (HR) decelerations. A specific 10 Hz Dash rTMS protocol (‘neuro-cardiac guided rTMS version 2.0’, NGC-2.0 rTMS) has been proposed to induce coupling of TMS and HR changes (heart-brain coupling; HBC).  This research encompasses two studies aimed at exploring the effects of NGC-TMS targeting the DLPFC. In the Study-1, we will replicate and corroborate previous findings with a larger cohort of twenty healthy young participants. These participants will undergo NGC-TMS sessions targeting the DLPFC, supplemented by sham TMS, across three sessions. Following these findings, the Study-2 will examine the robustness of HBC by assessing various stimulation intensities by targeting the most effective target identified in the Study-1.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Ferguson and Sheldon (2013)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Study Information
Trying to be happier really can work: Happiness and paintings
Conceptual Replication of Ferguson, Yuna & Sheldon, Kennon. (2013). Trying to be happier really can work: Two experimental studies. The Journal of Positive Psychology. 8. 23-33. 10.1080/17439760.2012.747000. 

Authorship
Brianna Chmielewski, Kamila Plaza, Meagan Rosario, Tyra Watkins
Research Questions

1.	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
2.	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
3.	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

Hypotheses
•	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
More specifically, do emotionally encouraged versus not encouraged groups feel more or less happy when analyzing an “ambiguous” and “happy” painting?
Our hypothesis is that the manipulation will be very effective. In the original study by Ferguson and Sheldon (2013), those who were part of the encouraged-to-improve-mood group felt a greater boost in mood when they listened to the positive classical song (p= 0.001, d= 0.76) and felt less of a positive mood when they listened to the ambiguous classical song (p= 0.72, d= 0.08). There was no difference in reported mood for the ambiguous song based on the group they were in (p= 0.82, d= 0.05).
•	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
	
Our hypothesis is that those viewing the positive image will report higher levels of mood compared to those viewing the ambiguous image. In the original study, Ferguson and Sheldon (2013) found that there was a significant effect of type of music on positive mood (p = .002). Since this is a conceptual replication, we expect to see similar results as this study. 

•	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

We expect to see those in the encouraged condition will be more impacted if in the positive condition rather than the ambiguous condition. We expect to see this because similar results were found in Ferguson and Sheldon’s study (2013). 

Sampling Plan
Data collection procedures

We plan to collect our data by using convenience sampling on students at Dominican University. Participants will be recruited by letting friends know about the study and asking our professors to send information to other classes to maximize our recruitment. There will be no compensation for this study other than credit that will be awarded to those currently enrolled in PSYC 101 and/or NEUR 105. Participants will be excluded from the initial pool if they fail the manipulation check or if they do not complete a substantial portion of the survey.
Sample size
Sample goal is at least 100 participants.
Sample size rationale
Based on the Dominican University population, we predicted that a sample size of at least 100 participants will satisfy our study to get an acceptable amount of results. 
Stopping rule
Sample size will not be limited to a certain amount; the more participants, the better. 

Variables
Manipulated variables
•	Type of images (ambiguous or happy) 
•	Encouraged to boost mood vs not encouraged to boost mood
Measured variables
•	How participants felt after viewing their assigned image. 
 2 measures:  
→ Rate their agreement (1= not at all, 15= extremely) on six different mood descriptors: happy, joyful, enjoyment/fun, pleased, content, and satisfied. Ratings were averaged.
→  Continuous line asked participants to indicate how positive they felt (line extended from “very negative” to “very positive”) relative to their negative feelings. Distance between positive and negative marks was measured using a ruler and converted into a proportion of entire line. 
 
Design Plan
Blind
Both the researchers and the participants are blind to the image manipulation. Computers will not be assigned to specific images, therefore we will not know who is in what group, and the participants will not be aware of the ambiguous and happy images until debriefing. 
Study design
2 x 2 factorial between-subject design .
Participants are randomly assigned within the online survey. 
Analysis Plan
Statistical models
TWO-WAY ANOVA

•	2x2 factorial ANOVA 
•	Analyze main effects and interactions between the two groups

Data exclusion

•	Participants who do not finish the survey.
•	Participants under the age of 18
•	Participants who do not pass the manipulation check.
•	Any participant who voices suspicion about the nature of the study
Missing data
Excluding participants entirely (except if missed demographic questions).

title_r: Direct replication of Staw (1976)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Escalation of commitment refers to the decision error in which people stick to their original decision despite negative feedback (Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara & Miles, 2012; Staw, 1976; Staw & Fox, 1977). In 1976, Staw initiated experimental research on escalating commitment. In his study Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action, he showed that escalation was particularly pronounced when people were personally responsible for negative decision consequences. The interaction between responsibility and consequence was significant (p = <.019). Since then, there have been numerous studies investigating the escalation of commitment and the underlying effects. The findings are ambivalent, as the results often do not match or even contradict those of Staw (1976). There are many studies that used Staw's (1976) stimulus material, the A&S Financial Decision Case, or were based on his approach (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Armstrong, Coviello & Safranek, 1993; Bialek, Węgrzyn, & Meyers, 2021; Conlon & Parks, 1987; McCain, 1986; Morgan & Hansen, 2006; Pfeiffer, Schönborn, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt, 2007; Schoorman & Holahan, 1996; Schoorman, Mayer, Douglas & Hetrick, 1994; Singer, 1990; Singer & Singer, 1986). However, these studies did not test the interaction effect responsibility x consequence (Armstrong et al., 1993) and altered or excluded relevant aspects of the paradigm. For example, a different scenario and other variables were examined (Negrini, Riedl & Wibral, 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007) or the methodological approach was changed (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Bialek et al., 2021; Singer & Singer, 1986). For this reason, the planned study in the form of a direct replication should provide information on how robust and reliable Staw's (1976) results are if there are as few deviations as possible from the original study. Of particular interest is the replicability of the interaction effect personal responsibility x decision consequences. In addition, the reasons for the investment decisions are evaluated using content analysis. Armstrong et al. (1993) asked the participants to justify their decision, but did not analyze this. Other studies did not even include the justification in their design (Bialek et al., 2021; Negrini et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007; Singer & Singer, 1986). The planned study therefore extends the existing literature with a replication of the study by Staw (1976), which not only records the participants' reasons for their decisions, but also evaluates them using content analysis.

title_r: Social Distance and Preference for Visual and Verbal Mediums in Interpersonal Communication: A Conceptual Replication of Amit et al. (2013, Experiment 2)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The present study aims to conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope’s (2013, Experiment 2) study, which explored the effect of social (psychological) distance on peoples’ medium preferences for interpersonal communication. The results showed that participants preferred mediums dominated by pictures for socially ‘close’ targets and mediums dominated by words for socially ‘distant’ targets. These findings support construal level theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010) which propose that people use more abstract representations when mentalizing targets that are more psychologically distant. The current study will conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope (2013, Experiment 2) to assess the robustness of the original conclusions by using a set of new pretested experimental materials.

title_r: The effect of prompts on the sharing of news headlines in social media: a pre-registered replication study of Capraro and Celadin (2023).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Misinformation, such as fake news and conspiracy theories, is contaminated among information on the internet. Specifically, research has found that 40% of information in the medical domain from the internet has been found to be misinformation (Waszak et al., 2018).
Today, various studies are being conducted to help prevent the spread of such misinformation. For example, increasing the sharing of accurate information by having people assess the accuracy of another article before a sharing task (Pennycook et al., 2020) or giving simple online literacy tips can reduce the sharing of misinformation (Epstein et al., 2021). Such methods of manipulating sharing on SNSs have been demonstrated.
However, while misinformation can be reduced, it is challenging to encourage the sharing of correct information. Capraro and Celadin (2023) found that adding a short sentence (prompt) to the 'share' option presented in the sharing task increased the sharing of correct information and reduced the sharing of misinformation. However, the participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, resulting in a biased sample. Therefore, to confirm the generalizability of Capraro and Celadin’s (2023) findings, the present study will conduct a replication study using a different sample to examine the viability of a method that promotes sharing of correct information and reduces the sharing of misinformation.

title_r: Testing the Replicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior: A Large-Scale Multi-Sample Registered Replication Study
abstract_r: Identifying the determinants of social behavior, and the specific processes by which the determinants relate to behavior, are important in the development of theory to predict social behavior. Predicting behavior also has utility for organizations and stakeholders interested in developing effective interventions and strategies to promote behavior change. The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) is a prominent social psychological theory developed to predict social behavior. The theory derives its assumptions from theories of attitude and social cognition (Albarracín & Johnson, 2019; Eagly & Chaiken, 1993; Fishbein, 1967), and focuses on predicting intentional behavior from sets of beliefs about future behavioral engagement. The theory has been tested in over 2000 studies, and over 30 meta-analytic syntheses. Cumulative findings indicate its efficacy in accounting for variance in behaviors across multiple domains. However, considerable unresolved heterogeneity in effects has been observed, which could be attributable to methodological artifacts or genuine variability across contexts, behaviors, and populations. In addition, some theory predictions, particularly interactions among constructs, have not been tested and replicated consistently. The current project will conduct a large-scale replication of the theory in general population and student samples adopting an identical protocol and measures. The result of the study will be a series of data sets testing theory predictions analyzed by meta-analytic structural equation modeling.

title_r: Perceived Personality Change Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: SEE WORD DOCUMENT FILE FOR FORMATTED SUBMISSION THAT INCLUDES TABLES/FIGURES

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from. 

Known differences from original studies: Herbst and colleagues (2000) used the NEO-PI-R whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have factor convergences ranging from .71 to .84 without correcting for attenuation (Reynolds & Clark, 2001). The study duration (theirs: 6 to 9 years versus ours: 4 years) and sample descriptives (theirs: middle-aged college alumni versus ours: current college students) will differ between studies. 

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

Both of these studies used a subset of data from a parent study, both of which differed in the sort of variables collected from our parent study.

Name or brief description of dataset: The present study uses a subset of data collected from the “College Life Study.” The parent study was designed as a longitudinal study of college student adjustment and development.

Is this data open or publicly available? The variables used in these analyses will be posted when the paper is submitted.

How can the data be accessed? Robert Ackerman and Courtney Brecheen collected these data.

Date of download or access: Andrew Rakhshani and Richard Lucas will access these data after submission of this registration.

Is a codebook available? Packets of questionnaires and data keys are available upon request. 

How was data collected? 
Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016: Data for this study come from an ongoing longitudinal study of college students at a public university in the Southwestern United States. Participants were initially recruited for the study toward the end of their first semester in their first-year orientation classes. Data for the current report were drawn from 1,158 total responses from college students ages 18 or older at the first wave of the study. Responses from 27 participants were discarded because they failed to answer affirmatively to a question “I answered all of these questions honestly” (25 responded “no” and 2 were missing responses). An additional 4 participants were discarded because they failed to answer any of the RSES items. Thus, the final sample size was 1,127 (55% men). Participants self-identified as Asian (38%), Anglo (39%), Hispanic (15%), African American (3%), or other or unknown (5%). The average age of the sample was 18.31 years (SD = 1.56, minimum = 18, maximum = 52, median = 18, mode = 18).

Have any of the authors worked with this dataset? 
Brent Donnellan, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman: Have published from the first wave of this study (Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016) and that study used the Big Five as criterion variables. Brent helped select measures for the study when it was being designed by Robert Ackerman with Courtney Brecheen. However, this registration and subsequent analyses will be completed by Richard Lucas and Andrew Rakhshani.
	Richard Lucas: No
	Andrew Rakhshani: No

What prior knowledge do the authors have about the dataset?
	Brent Donnellan, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman: Aware of the internal 
consistency estimates and stability coefficients for the Big Five domains. Aware of the distributions for the anticipated change items at Wave 1 and the perceived change items at the last wave. These have not been discussed with Andrew; these were discussed with Rich a long time ago, but he “does not recall this at all.” 
	Richard Lucas:  Reviewed the Time 1 and Time 8 questionnaire packets.
	Andrew Rakhshani: Reviewed the Time 1 and Time 8 questionnaire packets.

Sample size / Power analyses:
What is the sample size (to the best of your knowledge)? Number of complete BFIs:
	Time 1: 1267		Time 2: 361		Time 3: 450		Time 4: 277
	Time 5: 330		Time 6: 334		Time 7: 302		Time 8: 253
For the Robins et al. (2005) replication, we will only include participants that were 18 or 19 years old at wave one. This will remove very few participants so the above sample sizes should not change much.

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from.

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

summary: This registration preregisters our data collection and analysis plan for a replication of Eskine, Racinik, and Prinz (2011) at Tufts University (Spring, 2017). This plan was approved by the Collaborative Replication and Education Project team on Wed, Mar 8, 2017. Data collection, which has not yet begun, is slated to start as early as Fri, Mar 10, 2017. For full details, see the Wiki for this project, from which the following description of research questions and hypotheses was excerpted:

Research Questions

In this study, we will closely replicate an experiment reported by Eskine, Racinik, and Prinz (2011) . Eskine, Kacinik, and Prinz (2011) tested the hypothesis that moral judgments are influenced by our current emotional state. In their experiment, participants consumed a couple of swigs of a bitter, disgusting drink (Swedish Bitters), a sweet sugary drink (Minute Maid Berry Punch), or a neutral drink (water). Participants then evaluated the moral wrongness of a series of hypothetical scenarios. Results suggested that participants who drank the disgusting drink evaluated the behavior portrayed in the scenarios as significantly more morally wrong compared to participants who drank the sweet or neutral drinks. The authors further found some evidence to suggest that political orientation moderated this effect.

There are three reasons why this work is a great candidate for replication, especially in the context of a laboratory class this semester at Tufts University, PSY 42, Emotion Laboratory. First, the main objective of my emotion laboratory class is to teach students how to do research that examines the influence of emotion on behavior; the topic of this study perfectly fits the bill. Second, this study is one of several candidates for replication featured as part of the Collaborative Replication and Education Project (CREP) . CREP uses crowdsourcing to encourage replication by undergraduate researchers. It is a study that has been approved by IRBs and conducted by undergraduate researchers at a number of academic institutions, including Illinois Institute of Technology, Southern Oregon University, Wesleyan University, University of Minnesota, and others. Third, a replication that draws on a larger sample size will enable us to estimate the size of the effect with greater precision.

Hypotheses

This replication will test the same hypotheses examined by Eskine and colleagues (2011). They reported their hypotheses on page 296 as follows:

"If moral disgust really does stem from physical disgust, we hypothesized, then taste perception should affect moral processing such that a disgusting beverage should elicit greater moral disgust than a sweet beverage or a control beverage (water).

We hypothesized that if conservatives are indeed more sensitive to disgust, then the taste manipulation should affect their moral processing more strongly than the moral processing of liberals."

title_r: Foodie Calls - A Preregistered Replication Study
abstract_r: When it comes to the question of who is going to pay on a first date, it is not always clear how the bill is shared. While the consensus is hard to reach in many societies, gender roles, which are greatly impacted by culture, play a huge role in determining the answer to this highly debated question. In societies where traditional gender roles and norms are clearly defined and exercised, it might be expected that it is usually men who pay the bill on a first date (Delucia, 1987; Jaramillo-Sierra &amp; Allen, 2013; Wu et al., 2021). In a study based on a US sample, Collisson and colleagues (2020) reported that some women, especially the ones with dark personality traits and traditional gender role beliefs are prone to abuse men in order to receive a free meal on a first date without feeling any actual romantic attraction. However, the impact of Dark Triad personality traits might be irrelevant in circumstances, if traditional gender roles are more explicitly pronounced in society because of the expected norms that suggest men should always pay. The aim of this study is to test the impact of the Dark Triad personality traits on the “foodie call” behavior, which refers to the situation “where a person, despite a lack of romantic attraction to a suitor, chooses to go on a date to get a free meal” (Collisson et al., 2020, p. 425). The study is designed as a pre-registered replication study. The materials are presented on the OSF website.

Abstract (as of 6/1/20): 

In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.
