abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Title
Does thinking a product is lower priced make you enjoy taste less?

Original Study: Does more expensive wine actually taste better than cheap wine?
Goldstein, R., Emerson, J. W., & Katz, J. (2008). AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF WINE ECONOMISTS Editor DO MORE EXPENSIVE WINES TASTE BETTER ? EVIDENCE FROM A LARGE SAMPLE OF BLIND TASTINGS. Program, (16).
Authorship
Khadijah Alfred, Milena Collazo , Tiffany Ksiazek, Sheila Mendoza, and Alexandra Valenzuela
Research Questions
Does higher priced labeled brands taste better than lower priced labeled brands?
For this experiment, our interest was to see if the pricing and labeling of the brand's altered participants ratings of each cereal administered. However, participants were given two placebo conditions which were the label, of the average cost: Cheerios, and the high cost: Organic Morning O's, which actually contained the low cost: Great Value Cheerios.
Since we are looking for competency of higher priced items being preferred, participants who categorize incorrectly, and answer the hypothesis of the study correctly will be excluded from the analysis.
Recent research has shown that individuals appreciate the same wine more when they think that it is more expensive (Brochet, 2001; Plassmann et al., 2008). In other words, the price of a good affects the experienced utility derived from that good.
Researchers based this study on one set of experiments showed that the same wine, when thought to cost $45 vs. $5, was not only rated better by tasters but actually lit up the pleasure center of their brains more. In reality, the experiment gave the same wine to people, which resulted in them enjoying the $45 labeled one (Harding, 2014).
Hypotheses
•	Does higher priced labeled brands taste better than lower priced labeled brands?
Our hypothesis is that the manipulation will be very effective, that consumers will rate taste of the higher priced labeled to be higher than the lower priced labeled brands.  In the original study, For non-experts, the relationship between price and overall rating is negative; for experts, however, this is not the case. Our estimates of Model 2 show that the correlation between price and overall rating is positive – or, at any rate, non-negative – for experts. If we didn’t do this, we would be expecting a one dollar increase to have the same effect at the $5 price level as at the $50 price level. We get similar qualitative results using the dollar prices, but the statistical significance of the coefficients is not as good (but still significant) (R. Goldstein, J, et al., 2008). The price coefficient for non-experts is still negative, of about the same size as before, and with greatly improved statistical significance. The coefficient on the ln(price)*expert interaction term is highly statistically significant p-value: 0.017; OLS p-value: 0.015). For experts, the net coefficient on price is the sum of the two, i.e., about 0.11 for the ordered probit and 0.09 for OLS. This net coefficient is significantly different from zero, but only at the 10% level (p-value: 0.099; OLS p-value: 0.095), despite the large sample size. 
Sampling Plan
Data collection procedures
A convenience sample of students at the host institution will be collected. Participants will be recruited via a psychology participation pool and via direct solicitation by research assistants. Participants will receive a credit towards research participation requirements. The participants will be recruited from Dominican University, who are at least 18 years of age or older. Participants will be led to complete the experiment in a Parmer 209, which is considered a control setting environment. Each participant will be assigned a cubicle of their own where they will be given cheerios and administered a survey through Qualtrics. There will be compensation from this study for Nuero 105 and Psych 101 students at Dominican University.
Procedures:
The material being used for manipulation is a knock off brand of cheerios, Great Value O’s, but participants will believe that they are eating three different cheerio brands, the cheap brand (Great Value O’s Cereal), the original (Cheerios), and the organic brand (Organic Morning O's). This experiment will be taking place at Dominican University, in a control setting environment. Participants would be led to a private cubicle that contains a personal computer and pre-filled cups of Cheerios. Participants will then be presented with the three different cheerio brands within their cubicle. The lowest price brand condition is the cheerio brand that will actually contain its specific brand. In the placebo conditions, the plastic cups will be filled with the exact same Great Value Nut O's Cheerio brand. Before beginning the experiment participants will be asked to go onto the computer provided within their cubicle and consent to the experiment. Once the participant has consented, they will then be able to start eating the cheerios administered. When eating from both placebo conditions, participants will perceive they are eating the Cheerios, and Organic Morning O's. As a control, water will be administered to participants between each time of consumption. Participants in all conditions will be informed that the purpose of the study was for them to evaluate the quality of the Cheerios and will be instructed to consume the entire glass of water after each brand consumption.
However, the only type of cereal that is going to be administered, is the Great Value Cheerios, in which participants will perceive that they are trying three different types of cheerio brands. After that, participants will be asked to complete a survey online to rate the quality of each brand. Within the cubicles participants will have access to a computer where the survey will be administered, all the participant has to do is complete the survey. At the beginning of the survey participants will be asked to complete a basic demographic section which will contain age, year, gender. The next section, participants will consume and rate the taste of each brand. The participants will be presented with images. Each group of participants will receive randomized order of images for the cereal brands.  This is to make sure our experiment incorporates counterbalancing because it is a within subject’s design. The third section, participants will be asked to complete the manipulation check, in which they rate the prices. After that, participants will be asked a distractor question, what type of milk do they like to drink and add into their cereal. For the distractor question, the answers will be ignored by the researchers when analyzing the data.  Finally, the participants will be asked to guess the hypothesis of the experiment. Anyone who guesses that there is a relationship between price and quality will be excluded.
Sample size
Sample goal is 250 participants, which is approximately half of the original study’s sample size of 506. 
Sample size rationale
The sample size goal is based on Simonsohn’s guideline (2015) of collecting 2.5x original sample size to ensure good power (80%) for the smallest effect size credibly detectable with the original sample (smallest effect size of 33% power for original N). Usually the goal is to be 2.5x bigger than the original study but given the small participant pool from convenience sampling at Dominican University it can be difficult to receive 1000 participants.  
Stopping rule
Once sample size target of 250 is met, no more sessions will be scheduled or advertised, but those already scheduled will be completed. 
Variables
Manipulated variables
•	Images of cereal brands, as a means to manipulate perceived low to high cost labeled brands.  
Measured variables

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”.
We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. 
We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

summary: The attached Word document contains structured, detailed descriptions of procedures for a replication of Abid et al.'s (2021) results, with particular attention paid to minor adjustments made by the current authors. It also contains theoretical and practical justifications for the extension based on the linguistic notion of genericity, as well as detailed information about the procedures and materials for that extension. Potential follow-up experiments are also mentioned.

title_r: Tackett lab hormones replication project
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The present study is an attempt to reproduce, in an independent pre-adolescent sample, analyses from three studies examining the interaction between personality traits and hormones in predicting youth externalizing behavior.  The three papers are as follows: 

A. Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., & Tackett, J. L. (2015). Adolescent personality as risk and resiliency in the testosterone-externalizing association. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 26, 390-402.

B. Tackett, J. L., Herzhoff, K., Harden, K. P., Page-Gould, E., & Josephs, R. A. (2014). Personality x hormone interactions in adolescent externalizing psychopathology. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment. 5, 235-246. 

C. Tackett, J. L., Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., Page-Gould, E., Harden, K. P., & Josephs, R. A. (2015). Estradiol and cortisol interactions in youth externalizing psychopathology. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 55, 146-153. 

Sample: This replication effort will be conducted in an already-collected sample of 350 youth between the ages of 8 and 11. 

Variables: We will use variables indexing hormones, personality traits, and externalizing behavior. 

1. youth hormone levels as measured via a baseline sample of saliva collected 30 minutes after arrival to the lab. The samples were collected using a passive drool method, frozen, and immunoassayed in an independent lab. We will use the measurements of cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol (E2). 

2. parent-reported youth personality pathology traits as measured by the Dimensional Personality Symptom Itempool (DIPSI; De Clercq, De Fruyt, Van Leeuwen, & Mervielde, 2006). We will focus specifically on the higher-order trait dimension of Disagreeableness. 

3. parent-reported youth behavior as measured by the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). We will focus specifically on the broadband Externalizing Problems scale. 

Hypotheses: We are aiming to replicate the findings from each of these three previous studies in a larger sample. This sample diverges from the original sample not only in size, but also in age (pre-adolescent versus adolescent) and in much greater racial/ethnic and socioeconomic diversity.

A. Reardon et al., 2015: This study demonstrated that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only for youth with low levels of self-regulatory personality. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be predictive of externalizing behavior, but only for those youth high on disagreeableness. We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

B. Tackett, J. L., Herzhoff, K., Harden, K. P., Page-Gould, E., & Josephs, R. A. (2014). Personality x hormone interactions in adolescent externalizing psychopathology. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment. 5, 235-246. 

C. Tackett, J. L., Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., Page-Gould, E., Harden, K. P., & Josephs, R. A. (2015). Estradiol and cortisol interactions in youth externalizing psychopathology. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 55, 146-153. 

Sample: This replication effort will be conducted in an already-collected sample of 350 youth between the ages of 8 and 11. 

Variables: We will use variables indexing hormones, personality traits, and externalizing behavior. 

1. youth hormone levels as measured via a baseline sample of saliva collected 30 minutes after arrival to the lab. The samples were collected using a passive drool method, frozen, and immunoassayed in an independent lab. We will use the measurements of cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol (E2). 

2. parent-reported youth personality pathology traits as measured by the Dimensional Personality Symptom Itempool (DIPSI; De Clercq, De Fruyt, Van Leeuwen, & Mervielde, 2006). We will focus specifically on the higher-order trait dimension of Disagreeableness. 

3. parent-reported youth behavior as measured by the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). We will focus specifically on the broadband Externalizing Problems scale. 

Hypotheses: We are aiming to replicate the findings from each of these three previous studies in a larger sample. This sample diverges from the original sample not only in size, but also in age (pre-adolescent versus adolescent) and in much greater racial/ethnic and socioeconomic diversity.

A. Reardon et al., 2015: This study demonstrated that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only for youth with low levels of self-regulatory personality. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be predictive of externalizing behavior, but only for those youth high on disagreeableness. We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: The effect of selective spatial attention on the development of secondary hyperalgesia: a replication study
abstract_r: Cognitive factors, such as attention, play an important role in the modulation of pain and in the development of pain chronicity. We attempt to replicate one such effect found in a previous study conducted by Filbrich et al., 2020, which shows how the experimental induction of central sensitization, a key factor in the development of secondary hyperalgesia, can indeed be modulated by selective spatial attention. Secondary hyperalgesia occurs after tissue injury. It refers to a condition of increased sensitivity to mechanical stimuli within the injured area and the surrounding skin. It is hypothesized that the intense and sustained activation of peripheral nociceptors enhances the responsiveness of the neurons in the central nervous system. This causes the phenomenon known as central sensitization which is considered to play a key role in the development of chronic pain. As in Filbrich (2020), we will manipulate the impact of selective spatial attention by asking healthy volunteers to selectively focus their attention on target stimuli applied on one of the two forearms while we apply high frequency stimulation on both forearms. To assess the effect of the manipulation, we will measure perceived intensity to mechanical pinprick stimuli on both arms at three different moments: at T0, before applying high-frequency stimulation (HFS), at T1, immediately after having applied HFS in combination with the selective attention task, and finally at T2, 20 minutes after the whole procedure. Moreover, at T2, we will estimate the extent of the area of secondary hyperalgesia on both arms by applying mechanical pinprick stimulation along two axes: (1) medial-later, and (2) proximal-distal. title_r: GW4 21-22: Devaluation effects in food-specific response inhibition training: An independent conceptual replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Food-specific inhibitory control training (F-ICT) is a behavioural intervention in which participants learn to associate certain food-types with the inhibition of behaviour. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of such training in reducing food evaluations (e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018; Veling et al., 2013a), changing food choices (e.g., Veling et al., 2013b; Veling, Chen, et al., 2017), decreasing food intake (e.g., Lawrence, Verbruggen, et al., 2015; also see Allom et al., 2016) and even promoting weight loss (Lawrence, O’Sullivan, et al., 2015; Nederkoorn et al., 2010; Veling et al., 2014; see Jones et al., 2016 for a meta-analysis). This has led some researchers to suggest that F-ICT may be a cost-effective intervention with clinical utility (Carbine & Larson, 2019; Jones et al., 2016, 2018). 

One explanation for the effectiveness of F-ICT on health-related outcomes is provided by the Behaviour Stimulus Interaction (BSI) theory (Chen et al., 2016; Veling et al., 2008; Veling, Lawrence, et al., 2017), which proposes that during training food stimuli are devalued to reduce the response conflict caused by the need to inhibit motor responses towards (highly) appetitive items and thus facilitate task performance. In a series of six experiments using the Go/No-Go Task, Chen et al. (2016) examined the effect of of food-specific response inhibition training on stimulus devaluation by pairing appetitive stimuli with cues to respond (go stimuli) or with cues to not respond (no-go cues or the absence of cues). Providing evidence of stimulus devaluation, findings indicated that attractiveness ratings of no-go foods reduced after training whilst ratings of go-foods increased. This effect was then replicated in two preregistered experiments (Chen, Veling, Dijksterhuis, et al., 2018) and across obese and normal-weight individuals (Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018), showing consistently that no-go foods were rated as less attractive post-training compared to go-foods and untrained foods. 

The aim of the current study is to conceptually replicate the devaluation effect found by Chen et al. (2016) for food attractiveness ratings in a high-powered and representative sample, as well as exploring potential moderators of these effects.

title_r: Self Regulation Ontology Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Previously (Eisenberg et al., 2019), our lab leveraged exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on the dependent variables (n=193 DVs) extracted from 522 individuals’ performances on a large range of tasks (n=37 tasks, n=129 DVs) and self-report surveys (n=22 surveys, n=64 DVs) broadly related to the psychological construct of ‘Self Regulation’. While 12 factors were recovered from the survey DVs, only 5 factors were recovered from task-derived DVs. of the 5 task factors, 3 (speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response) were strongly related to DVs that were parameters of drift diffusion modeling (DDM): drift rate, threshold, and non-decision time, respectively. This may indicate that DDM captures fundamental dimensions of cognition. Alternative, this could suggest that examining the data through the lens of DDM conceals otherwise fundamental cognitive factors that are central to other taxonomies in the literature (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000), like shifting, updating, and inhibition. 
	To investigate these possibilities, we plan to perform EFA and the subsequent analyses of Eisenberg et al. (2019) on the original data, replacing the DDM parameters with reaction time, accuracy, and within-subject reaction time standard deviation. We propose two competing hypothesis classes.  First, the factors recovered could be similar in number and occupy a similar factor space and axes as the original factors. For example, we could again find a 5-factor solution, but dependent variables that previously loaded on speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response may now load onto RT variance, accuracy, and mean reaction time, respectively. Within this class, a more specific outcome would be that these new factors provide worse fits to the data than the original factors. This would indicate that the additional assumptions of the DDM combined with the original modeling parameters produce dependent variables which better reflect the underlying psychological factor space. Alternatively, the new factors could better fit the data compared to the old factors, indicating that the additional assumptions of DDM distort the data in some way, and would encourage further investigation. 
	Second, the new factor solution may be fundamentally different in factor number and factor space/axes. For example, the original 5-factor solution may give way to a higher-dimensional solution in which dependent variables map onto more traditional psychological constructs like attention, working memory, shifting, inhibition, etc.  Alternatively, we may recover a set of factors more obscure that do not map cleanly onto the original factor solution or existing taxonomies of cognitive processes (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000). 
	The first class of hypotheses would provide evidence that the Eisenberg et al. (2019) ontology is robust to the presence or absence of the DDM modeling and transformation of the raw reaction and accuracy data. Alternatively, the second class of hypotheses would suggest that the ontology (Eisenberg et al., 2019) is more idiosyncratic to analytical decisions like whether to analyze the data through the lens of the DDM.

Close Replication of Muñoz, De Los Reyes: The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships

item29: 1.	Verbal description of the effect I am trying to replicate (optional)  The study “The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships” by Muñoz and De Los Reyes (2021) examined the connection between the three traits of the dark triad (i.e., Psychopathy, Machiavellianism and Narcissism) and honesty rule endorsement in romantic relationships, defined as obligatory rules and discretionary rules. Obligatory rules consist of strict standards for honest communication, while discretionary rules provide the flexibility to determine when deception is appropriate. We are trying to replicate the following hypotheses:  1.	High Psychopathy positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement.  2.	High Psychopathy negatively predicts obligatory rule endorsement.  3.	High Machiavellianism positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement. 4.	Narcissism shows no effects on either honesty rule endorsement.   2.	It is important to replicate this effect because (optional)  With the replication crisis in mind, it is important to strengthen the confidence in the reliability of the reported effects, so that this replication study should promote the confidence in the postulated relationships between the dark triad traits and honesty rule endorsement (Brandt, 2014).  Further, in the original study, 98.05% of the participants were Hispanics and most of the participants were female. Thus, this replication study which will be conducted with a German sample and a more balanced gender ratio will help to answer the question concerning the generalizability of the findings of the original study to other contexts.   3.	The effect size of the effect I am trying to replicate is (optional)  1.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .26.  2.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and obligatory rule endorsement is r = -.10. This effect is mentioned as significant in the text but not in the attached bivariate correlation matrix.  3.	The effect size of the effect between Machiavellianism and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .28.  4.	The confidence interval of the original effect is (optional)  Not specified   5.	The sample size of the original effect is (optional)  Two different sample sizes are reported in the paper. According to the text, the sample size is N = 257, but according to the bivariate correlation matrix, the sample size is N = 258.    6.	Where was the original study conducted? (e.g., lab, in the field, online) (optional)  The original study was conducted online.   7.	What country/region was the original study conducted in? (optional)  The researchers are from University of Texas, but it is not clear in the text where the study was conducted in.  8.	What kind of sample did the original study use? (e.g. student, Mturk, representative) (optional)  The original sample consisted of n = 221 females, n = 35 males, n = 1 or 2 other (see Point 5). 95.33% of the participants were between 18 and 29 years old and 98.05% self-identified as Hispanic. No further information were given.  9.	Was the original study conducted with paper-and-pencil surveys, on a computer, or something else? (optional)  The original study was conducted on a computer.    Designing the Replication Study  10.	Are the original materials for the study available from the author? (optional)  -	No  11.	I know that assumptions (e.g., about the meaning of the stimuli) in the original study will also hold in my replication because (optional)  We will use validated and empirically tested questionnaires. For the assessment of the Dark Triad character traits, we will use the Short Dark Triad (SD3; Jones & Paulhus, 2014) which includes 9 items each for Machiavellianism, Narcissism and Psychopathy. It was already translated to German so we will use the translated version (Malesza et al., 2017). The other questionnaire we will use is a measure of honesty rules endorsement in relationships which includes 21 obligatory rule statements and 22 discretionary rule statements (Roggensack & Sillars, 2014). This questionnaire is written in English, so we will translate it to German. The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted. For both questionnaires we will use a 5-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). We will also ask for participants age, culture and gender to rule out any impact on the effect.  12.	Location of the experimenter during data collection (optional)  Not applicable   13.	Experimenter knowledge of participant experimental condition (optional)  Not applicable   14.	Experimenter knowledge of overall hypotheses (optional)  All experimenters know about all hypotheses.   15.	My target sample size is (optional)  Our target sample size is N = 256, but we will collect N = 270 participants because of possible exclusions.  16.	The rationale for my sample size is (optional)  An a priori power analysis for correlation was conducted, assuming an effect size of r = .26 (which was smallest significant effect reported in the original study), setting Type I error rate at  = .05 and power at 99%.    Documenting Differences between the Original and Replication Study  17.	The similarities/differences in the instruction are (optional)  -	Different  18.	The similarities/differences in the measures are (optional)  -	Close   19.	The similarities/differences in the stimuli are (optional)  Not applicable   20.	The similarities/differences in the location (e.g., lab vs. online; alone vs. in groups) are (optional)  -	Exact  21.	The similarities/differences in remuneration are (optional)  The remuneration is not given in the paper. There will be no remuneration in our replication.   22.	The similarities/differences between participant populations are (optional)  -	Close   23.	What differences between the original study and your study might be expected to influence the size and/or direction of the effect? (optional)  Because we do not have the original materials there might be differences in the instruction text of the study and as already mentioned (see Point 11), we will self-translate the English questionnaire for honesty rules endorsement in relationships to German.   24.	I have taken the following steps to test whether the differences listed in the previous question will influence the outcome of my replication attempt (optional)  The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted (see Point 11).  Analysis and Replication Evaluation  25.	My exclusion criteria are (e.g., handling outliers, removing participants from analysis) (optional)  We will exclude participants who don’t give their consent to participate and those who are younger than 18 years. If participants answer one of the attention check questions incorrectly, participants will be excluded afterwards.   26.	My analysis plan is (justify differences from the original) (optional)  First we will calculate descriptive statistics for all relevant variables (i.e, Machiavellianism, Psychopathy, Narcissism, obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement). Then, we will calculate an intercorrelation matrix for all relevant variables. Lastly, we will conduct two regression analyses with each trait of the dark triad as the predictor for obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement as dependent variables.   27.	A successful replication is defined as (optional)  We interpret our replication as success if the standard significance criterion (p < .05) is fulfilled and if the effect is in the same direction as the original effect (OSF, 2015).  28.	The finalized materials, procedures, analysis plan etc. of the replication are registered here:   We will use the OSF platform to register the necessary materials for the replication.

title_r: Psychometric Reliability of ERN and Pe Across Flanker, Stroop, and Go/No-Go Tasks: A Direct and Conceptual Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The purpose of this study is to replicate and extend work on the psychometric reliability of cognitive control event-related potentials (ERPs) as a function of increasing trials across three different tasks (Meyer et al., 2013, Psychophysiology). Our primary aim is a direct replication of Meyer et al. (2013) to determine the number of trials needed for adequate psychometric internal consistency (.70) of the error-related negativity (ERN) recorded during flanker, Stroop, and Go/no-go tasks using classical test theory estimates (i.e., coefficient alpha). Our second aim is to extend these findings by conducting a conceptual replication examining generalizability theory estimates of internal consistency (i.e., dependability) of ERN, correct-response negativity (CRN), post-error positivity (Pe), post-correct positivity (Pc), and their difference scores (ERN, Pe; error minus correct) as a function of the number of trials across the three tasks. We will use post-estimation contrasts to identify task differences in dependability and ICC estimates as function of the number of trials recoded.

title_r: The relationship between occipitotemporal sulcal morphology and children’s reading ability: a replication study
abstract_r: Recent literature suggested that interruption in the left posterior occipitotemporal sulcus (pOTS) is a prenatally determined predictor of reading ability in children and adults. Compared with those with a continuous left pOTS, participants with interruption in this region had better overall reading skills (Borst et al., 2016; Bouhali et al., 2024; Cachia et al., 2018). Here, we wish to replicate this finding in a larger sample of children and adolescents (N = 156) aged 10-15 years with a range of language-learning abilities. In addition to replication, we will also test the relationships between OTS sulcal morphology and other measures of language and cognition.

title_r: Extreme weather, climate change, climate action and uncertainty distress: A replication study using network analysis.
abstract_r: Both extreme weather and climate change have been linked to distress and at times mental health problems. Pro-environmental actions have often been related to higher distress. The uncertainty distress model (Freeston et al., 2020) proposes that in real-world situations, perceptions of threat and uncertainty contribute to distress. Freeston, Sermin-Read, et al. (2023) recruited a community sample (N = 327) who completed an online survey. Network analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the variables. Exposure to extreme weather, perceptions of climate change, climate change distress and pro-environmental action were measured along with symptoms of adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and uncertainty intolerance and behaviours. They reported there was variable exposure to extreme weather, but greater exposure was associated with more severe post-traumatic symptoms. Pro-environmental action was associated with greater severity of adjustment disorder symptoms. The perception that climate change was happening now was linked positively to pro-environmental action and negatively to perceptions of uncertainty about whether climate change was happening. The results replicated several findings from the emerging climate change distress literature and are consistent with some predictions of the uncertainty distress model, but not others. Aim: The main aim of the current study is to conduct a replication using network analysis with 1) improved measurement in some areas (see above and in measures section), 2) a larger and more diverse sample (see recruitment methods). The network analysis will follow the previous analysis as much as possible to facilitate comparison. Methods: The study will essentially replicate the previous study with the following modifications: inclusion of heatwaves; expand the type, timescale and impact of warnings; differentiated assessment of disruption; fuller range of emotional responses; shortened/improved versions of other measures. A larger sample will be sought, recruited to increase not only the diversity and representativeness of the sample, but also the geographical distribution and so the range of experiences of extreme weather. Results: Descriptive analyses of the participants, the experiences of extreme weather, and network analysis will be reported, based on the previous study.

title_r: Contralateral delay activity as a marker of visual working memory capacity: a multi-site registered replication
abstract_r: Visual working memory (VWM) is a temporary storage system capable of retaining information that can be accessed and manipulated by higher cognitive processes, thereby facilitating a wide range of cognitive functions. Electroencephalography (EEG) is used to understand the neural correlates of VWM with high temporal precision, and one commonly used EEG measure is an event-related potential called the contralateral delay activity (CDA). In a landmark study by Vogel and Machizawa (2004), the authors found that the CDA amplitude increases with the number of items stored in VWM and plateaus around three to four items, which is thought to represent the typical adult working memory capacity. Critically, this study also showed that the increase in CDA amplitude between two-item and four-item arrays correlated with individual subjects’ VWM performance. Although these results have been supported by subsequent studies, a recent study suggested that the number of subjects used in experiments investigating the CDA may not be sufficient to detect differences in set size and to provide a reliable account of the relationship between behaviorally measured VWM capacity and the CDA amplitude. To address this, the current study, as part of the #EEGManyLabs project, aims to conduct a multi-site replication of Vogel and Machizawa's (2004) seminal study on a large sample of participants, with a pre-registered analysis plan. Through this, our goal is to contribute to deepening our understanding of the neural correlates of visual working memory.

Kathryn V. Walter & Daniel Conroy-Beam

Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara 

Date pre-registered on the Open Science Framework: April 17, 2018
This document was fixed in its current form prior to data analysis, all later amendments will be visible.

Date Made Public: April 17, 2021

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

This document was fixed in its current form prior to data analysis, all later amendments will be visible.

Date Made Public: April 17, 2021

Correspondence regarding this pre-registration should be addressed to Kathryn V. Walter, Email: kathryn.walter@psych.ucsb.edu, or using the comment function on the Open Science Framework. 
Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.
 	For all cross-cultural comparisons, we will report both a base model with no controls and models that attempt to approximate relevant controls used in the original papers (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy. 
Pathogen Prevalence
We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). The third pathogen prevalence index will be a new index created by combining two variables from publicly available databases: years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (for all persons; WHO, 2015). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality 
To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. The gender equality variables used will be the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999); the updated GDI; the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI); and the Gender Inequality Index (GII), as well as a composite variable created through principal components analysis (PCA) using the updated GDI, GGGI, and GII. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

title_r: Amendment to Tremoliere_Cognition_2012_8wZ0 - Bagó_Aczel_276 - Direct Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This registration serves as an amendment to the focal hypothesis in the previously registered replication of a research claim from Trémolière et al. (2012), from Cognition. The original registration can be found here: https://osf.io/a7gd2.

summary: This registration serves as an amendment to our original preregistration (available here: https://osf.io/a7gd2). We have updated the SCORE focal hypothesis (H*) to more precisely define the pattern of findings expected for a replication.

The original H* was defined as: "a significant interaction between the mortality salience condition (death vs. pain, between subjects) and the scenario type (harm-conflict vs. harm control, within subjects), where the pattern of this interaction is such that people in the death condition are less likely to give utilitarian responses to the harm-conflict scenarios."

The pattern of findings expected for a replication have been more precisely defined as the following: "We expect that people in the death condition give less utilitarian response than people in the pain condition on the harm-conflict dilemmas, whereas we expect that there will be no (or significantly smaller) effect of death/pain condition on harm-control dilemmas."

We have collected about 2/3 of our intended final sample at the point of this amendment. We have reached our first stopping point (230 participants), where we found no significant interaction. Since this point, we collected 100 more participants, but have not yet computed the statistical test, nor did we look at the group level averages in any way.
