title_r: Study 1: Conceptual Replication of Children’s Preferences for Shared-Language Speakers
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Background.
This is a conceptual replication of the study conducted with 5-year-old children described in Kinzler et al. (2007). The original study showed 8 monolingual English-speaking children, two children speaking: one spoke in French and one in English. They found that participants preferred to have the child who spoke the same language as them (English) as their friend.

The purpose of this study is to conceptually replicate these findings with a different type of stimuli that we plan to use in a subsequent study with a different research question. Here, children will observe puppets speaking, instead of human children. We will ask if children prefer speakers of their shared language, even when the speakers are puppets.

Logic and Hypotheses.
Question: Will 4-to-5-year-old, monolingual English-speaking children choose English-speaking puppets as their friends?
Hypothesis: We expect that 4-to-5-year-old children will choose the English-speaking puppet to be their friend, in line with Kinzler et al.’s (2007) results.
Interpretation: If this is the case, we will interpret this as evidence that children prefer puppets who speak their language.
Alternative: If children choose both puppets equally often or choose the non-shared language puppet it would suggest they do not interpret the language spoken by puppets the same way as humans.

summary: Background.
This is a conceptual replication of the study conducted with 5-year-old children described in Kinzler et al. (2007). The original study showed 8 monolingual English-speaking children, two children speaking: one spoke in French and one in English. They found that participants preferred to have the child who spoke the same language as them (English) as their friend.

The purpose of this study is to conceptually replicate these findings with a different type of stimuli that we plan to use in a subsequent study with a different research question. Here, children will observe puppets speaking, instead of human children. We will ask if children prefer speakers of their shared language, even when the speakers are puppets.

Logic and Hypotheses.
Question: Will 4-to-5-year-old, monolingual English-speaking children choose English-speaking puppets as their friends?
Hypothesis: We expect that 4-to-5-year-old children will choose the English-speaking puppet to be their friend, in line with Kinzler et al.’s (2007) results.
Interpretation: If this is the case, we will interpret this as evidence that children prefer puppets who speak their language.
Alternative: If children choose both puppets equally often or choose the non-shared language puppet it would suggest they do not interpret the language spoken by puppets the same way as humans.

Sample Plan.
We will test at least 25 children, or until we reach a Bayes Factor of 10 for our alternative hypothesis, with a maximum of 50 children (refer to analyses below).  Participants will be monolingual English-speaking children (i.e., children exposed to English 90-100% of the time) based in the United States.

Participants.
Participants will be children of 4 and 5 years of age (i.e., 48 months and 0 days to and 71 months and 15 days) of age from the United States, expanding on the age found in previous literature to show a language-based social preference (Kinzler et al., 2007).

Design.
This study will take place via synchronous recorded online video-chat sessions to increase the accessibility of our research. Here, we measure children’s social preference for puppets who either share their language or do not share their language. The study will follow a within-subjects design, which means each participant will be shown two pairs of puppets.

Procedure.
Each child will be shown videos of two sets of puppets speaking towards the camera. In each set one of the puppets will speak the same language as the participant, (English) and one of the puppets will speak a different language (French or Hindi).

After each trial’s familiarization video, children will be played an audio clip of each puppet over a screenshot of the two puppets facing the camera. They will be asked “Which puppet sounded like this?” as an attention check to ensure they can accurately link the puppets with their respective shared and non-shared languages.

Then, accompanied by the same screenshot of the two puppets side-by-side, children will be asked the following questions: “Whom would you like to have as your friend?” and “Why is that?” (Kinzler et al., 2007).

Dependent Variables.
The primary dependent measure will be a 0-1 binary response of “shared” or “non-shared”. This refers to whether children select the puppet that spoke in English (shared language) or the puppet that spoke in Hindi or French (non-shared language) in response to the question, “Whom would you like to have as your friend?”.

Primary analysis.
To analyze the data, we will run one-sample one-sided Bayesian binomial tests for children’s responses in JASP (JASP Team, 2024), which compares the likelihood of the data given the null hypothesis that children will be at chance in choosing the puppets who share their language or not to the alternative hypothesis that children will choose the puppet who shares their language more than half of the time. We will look at the data as a whole (across both conditions) and within each condition.

Secondary Analyses.
Children’s Explanations: Exploratory qualitative analysis on the open-ended “Why?” question where children explain their choice.

In secondary analyses, we will compare across conditions (Hindi versus French). We will use a mixed effects model to test for effects of condition using the package brms: Outcome ~ Condition + (1 | Participant). Where, “Outcome” refers to whether participants chose the shared-language puppet, and “Condition” refers to the order of the puppets sets (English-French or English-Hindi first) and position and color of the shared-language puppet.

We will also test for order effects by running a model with Outcome ~ Condition*Order + (1 | Participant), where order is whether the Hindi or French condition came first, though we will likely be underpowered to find an interaction.
Decisions about whether a participant and/or participant test trial is excluded will be determined before their data are analyzed.

Exclusion Criteria.
Participant test trials will be marked as missing based on the following criteria:
Experimenter error (e.g., the experimenter goes off script); Not choosing one puppet or saying “I don’t know”; Giving two responses and not confirming a single answer on the binary measure; Parental or outside interference: (i.e., an individual tells the participant what response to say to the experimenter); Participants who are not between the ages of 4 years 0 months 0 days and 5 years 11 months 15 days; Children who fail the attention check questions after 2 repetitions.

Participants will be excluded and replaced if they meet any of the above criteria, either determined live at the time of the study or when reviewed after the experiment. 

Pilot data.
We initially ran a between-subjects pilot for this study. Nine out of 11 participants in this version chose the English-speaking puppet.

Next, we collected within-subjects (n=5) and found that 7 out of 10 choices were made in favor of the English-speaking puppet.

The current pilot data are trending towards the expected outcome, that monolingual English-speaking children will prefer the English-speaking puppet as their friend.

References.
Kinzler, K. D., Dupoux, E., & Spelke, E. S. (2007). native language of social cognition. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 104(30), 12577–12580. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0705345104

A pre-registration document which incudes the above summary and a full study appointment script is attached.

title_r: Does the corollary discharge provide the sensory content of inner speech? A preregistered direct replication and extension of Scott (2013)
abstract_r: The mental production of speech or "inner speech" is a remarkable and foundational ability in humans, involved in many daily activities such as reading, writing, remembering, or planning. Inner speech is generally accompanied by a subjective multisensory (mainly auditory) experience. However, the cognitive processes leading to these sensory percepts remain poorly known. One prominent perspective is that the sensory content of inner speech would correspond to the predicted sensory consequences of inhibited speech acts. Scott (2013) provided experimental evidence suggesting that inner speech indeed involves the mental simulation of speech acts, as evidenced by sensory attenuation of the concomitant perception of external speech sounds. However, Scott (2013) assessed silent speech, but not inner speech, which in contrast to silent speech, does not involve visible articulatory movements. The present work aims to replicate and extend the study of Scott (2013) to assess whether inner speech attenuates the perception of concomitant external speech sounds.

title_r: Assessment of research quality, scholarly productivity and citation impact of UK academic psychologists and clustering of UK universities into groupings: A replication and extension study.
abstract_r: It is no question that higher education institutions in the United Kingdom (UK) excel in research, development and innovation. Such productivity in the education sector massively contributes to economic growth, with the government investing billions of dollars each year to actively encourage research excellence (Hewitt-Dundas, 2012). A study by Mazzucchelli et al., (2019) examined the impact of research productivity of Australian academic psychologists and tried to understand how an increase in research productivity at universities forms the basis for judgments concerning various matters. They observed that academics in various university groupings (like the Group of Eight) and academic levels (professor, lecturer) differed in terms of lifetime citation, number of publications and h-index. These differences can have a two-fold impact - on an institutional level, these can influence rankings of universities, funding and prestige. On an individual academic’s level, research productivity informs decisions about job selection, career progression and research grant applications. The aim of this study is to understand if these findings replicate in the context of the United Kingdom by observing research patterns across various university groupings that exist in the United Kingdom (e.g. Russell group, Million Plus, GuildHE etc). In addition, this study will extend its research question by focusing its attention on the Russell group universities and examine their claim of “Research Excellence” by verifying if these universities appear together in a cluster when applying the statistical method of cluster analysis. Furthermore, we will compare the university grouping and academic levels in terms of their average publication quality (as operationalised by the SJR metric). We expect Russell Group universities and more senior academics to perform significantly better in this measure of quality. We may also run further exploratory analysis to understand the effects of other factors like gender on research performance on a global scale and compare pairs of university groupings to understand this phenomenon in depth. What does research productivity mean to us? Mazzucchelli et al., (2018) used an academic’s lifetime papers published, lifetime citations and h-index as quantitative indicators of research productivity. Building on the assumption that a high number of papers published does not necessarily mean that those papers are also of high standards, this study will go beyond by trying to assess the quality of their research productivity. A high-quality journal does not publish any and every paper. The highly selective nature of such journals makes them prioritize the quality of research as a prime factor before approving it for publication. The SJR developed by Scopus is a widely used proxy for research quality. The current study will attempt to assess the quality aspect of research productivity by comparing the average SJRs of papers published by academics at different seniority levels in different university groupings.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Functional Family Therapy-Gangs: Randomized Controlled Trial of Gang-Involved Youth on Pre-Trial and Probation Supervision in the Denver Area
abstract_r: This proposal focuses on Functional Family Therapy-Gangs (FFT-G), which is an extension of a therapeutic intervention targeting youth presenting problem behaviors—Functional Family Therapy (FFT)—that is designed to help troubled youth and their families overcome delinquency, substance abuse, and violence. In 2009, Drs. Thornberry and Gottfredson led an advisory group of leading prevention scientists and gang researchers in selecting FFT to adapt to address the severity of risk factors observed with gang populations, as a large body of research highlights the importance of household dynamics for youth gang members. The associated manual and trainings became known as FFT-G. A subsequent RCT of FFT-G with a sample of adjudicated youth in Philadelphia revealed reductions in recidivism over an 18-month period (Gottfredson et al., 2018) , . This study will replicate the study design and outcomes from Thornberry and Gottfredson’s evaluation by implementing FFT-G in the Denver area. We will target juveniles on pre-trial and probation supervision who are embedded in gangs, which is distinguishable from the Philadelphia evaluation, as 15% of their sample had ever been a member of a gang and only half maintained high gang risk. The FFT-G model is designed to serve the dual function of gang prevention and intervention. Thornberry and Gottfredson’s important work focused on the former; ours will focus on the latter. We will use official records in conjunction with youth and parent reports to compare outcomes 18 months after youth were assigned at random to FFT-G or treatment-as-usual (TAU) conditions.

title_r: Study 1 (Direct Replication)
abstract_r:
**CREP Project: #20-43** 
 
**PROTOCOL TITLE:**   
Evaluation of Meat Consumption 
 
**PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR (PI):**   
*Name:* Heather Urry   
*Department:* Psychology 
 
**Purpose of the study:** 
 
This study is a direct replication of one experiment from research conducted by Sparkman and Walton (2017) that investigated dynamic and static norms in relation to meat consumption. Our study aims to determine whether dynamic norms lead to a greater desire to change one’s eating habits than static norms.  
 
**Background / Literature Review / Rationale for the study:** 
 
In the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), the researchers found that participants were more interested in reducing their meat consumption if they first learned that norms for reducing meat consumption have been increasing over the past 5 years. This was compared to a condition in which there was no implied change; the norm was presented as static.  
 
We are replicating this study because the topic is of general interest and importance. In addition, this study is among those available for undergraduate student groups to replicate with faculty mentorship as part of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project.  
 
**Participant Population:** 
 
We will study adult participants currently in the United States who are at least 18 years old, each of whom may participate in the study just once. (Vegan/vegetarian participants will be excluded from analyses but not from participating in the study.) 
 
**Research Locations and Sample Size:** 
 
*Research Locations* 
 
This research will be administered online via a Qualtrics survey. Participants will complete it in a location of their choosing that offers a computer with internet access. 
 
*Sample Size* 
 
We seek to recruit at least 122 participants, the same number of participants studied by the original authors. A sample of 122 participants – 61 in each of two norm conditions – will give us 80% power to detect medium standardized effects of Cohen’s *d* = 0.51 or larger for the difference in self-reported interest between the dynamic and static conditions.   
 
The original authors reported an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.41. Ideally we’d have enough participants to detect an effect of that size with adequate power in this study. This would require 94 participants per group for a total of 188 participants.   
 
Even better, we should have enough participants to detect an effect that’s so small that the original authors would have been unlikely to detect it. To that end, Simonsohn (2015) suggests specifying in one’s power analysis an effect size the original authors could have detected with only 33% power.  In this case, with 118 participants included in the key analysis, the original authors had 33% power to detect an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.28.  To have 80% power to detect an effect size of *d* = 0.28 or larger, we would need to collect data from 201 participants per group for a total of 402 participants.  
 
Our maximum N will be 3,000.  
 
**Procedures Involved:** 
 
We are conducting a between-subjects experiment in which we will manipulate type of norm (dynamic, static). Participants will complete this research online via a Qualtrics survey. We anticipate that each participant will take 5-10 minutes to complete the study. The study will unfold over the course of the Fall 2020 semester.  
 
The survey will start by assessing the GeoIP location of potential respondents. For people whose GeoIP location suggests they are not currently in the United States, the survey will explain our eligibility criteria and then take the respondent to a message noting their ineligibility. Otherwise, the survey will proceed to the informed consent form. 
 
After providing informed consent, participants will respond to a Captcha verification item to prevent bot responses to the online survey. They will also provide answers to three eligibility items (age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) to prevent participation by people who are ineligible. Participants who are ineligible or decline to answer will then see a message explaining that they are ineligible.  
 
Participants who are eligible will then read instructions related to their randomly-assigned norm condition. In the static-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that 30% of Americans make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that 3 in 10 people eat less meat than they otherwise would.  
 
In the dynamic-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that, in the last 5 years, 30% of Americans have now started to make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that, in recent years, 3 in 10 people have changed their behavior and begun to eat less meat than they otherwise would. 
 
After reading the statement, each participant will respond to the following items: 
 
1.	How interested are you in eating less meat? (1 = not at all, 4 = somewhat, 7 = extremely). 
2.	Most people eat breakfast, lunch and dinner everyday. That means they eat 21 meals in a typical week. For those that make an effort to eat less meat, how many times do you think they eat a meal without meat in a week? 
3.	What percentage of people do you think make an effort to limit their meat consumption? 
4.	Which best describes your political ideology? (1 = very liberal, 7 = very conservative) 
5.	What word or phrase best describes your gender?  
6.	Are you vegetarian or vegan? 
7.	What is your current age in years? 
8.	What word or phrase best describes your race and/or ethnicity? 
9.	Did you participate to earn SONA credit or for a chance to enter a drawing? (SONA credit, Drawing, Neither; I'm volunteering) 
 
Finally, participants will see the debriefing form and an item in which they will have the option to exclude their data from the final data set, if they wish.  
 
Some items will require a response from participants; they will always have a “decline to answer” option so they are not compelled to provide information they do not wish to share. 
 
Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of entering a drawing will, upon clicking the survey submission button, be redirected to a new contact information survey in which they can provide their name and email address if they wish to be entered into a drawing to receive $50 as compensation. Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of SONA credit will receive 0.5 credits in the SONA credit system. 
 
Some pages in the survey will be set to measure the time participants spend on them for exploratory analyses.   
 
**Confirmatory Analyses:** 
 
We will exclude from analyses participants who identify as vegetarian/vegan, participants who decline to include their responses in the final data set after debriefing, participants who select the "decline to answer" option for key variables in each analysis, and participants who do not complete the survey through to the debriefing form and thus do not have the opportunity to withdraw their data. 
 
After applying these exclusions, we will repeat the same analyses reported by Sparkman and Walton (2017) as follows:  
 
1.	A t-test to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption.  
2.	A multiple regression to see if type of norm affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption when accounting for variation explained by gender and political orientation.  
3.	Two additional t-tests to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects estimates of the percentage of people who limit their meat consumption and the number of meatless meals per week eaten by people who say they limited their meat consumption. 
 
We will also report descriptive statistics and standardized effect sizes as reported by the original authors. 
 
In addition, we anticipate that there may be outlying observations or responses suggesting a lack of good-faith participation (e.g., based on open-ended information or extremely fast completion times). We may repeat our confirmatory analyses without these observations to see if conclusions change. 
 
**Known Deviations** 
 
1. We are recruiting participants in the United States, probably most of whom will be students at Tufts and/or people in the Boston area of Massachusetts. The original researchers recruited participants using Amazon's Mechanical Turk. 
2. We will offer participants the opportunity to enter a drawing for USD 50 dollars or to earn credit in partial fulfillment of course requirements as incentives to participate. In the original study, participants on Mechanical Turk received USD 25 cents. 
3. For our replication, the survey will include eligibility items (Captcha verification, age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) before participants complete the survey items that address confirmatory hypotheses. 
 
**Incomplete Disclosure or Deception:** 
 
In the consent form, we tell participants that we are not disclosing all information about the nature and purpose of the study and that, at the end of the study, they’ll receive a full explanation. Specifically, we do not disclose our specific focus on whether dynamic versus static norms influence interest in reducing meat consumption, or that we’re measuring how much time they spend on various pages of the survey and other variables of interest, as described above. This incomplete disclosure is necessary because full participant knowledge could impact their responses and compromise our results. We do not believe this incomplete disclosure violates the rights or welfare of participants because a) we correctly inform potential participants in the consent form that we’re conducting a study to evaluate meat consumption, b) we correctly inform participants about the general procedures of the study, namely that they’ll be completing a survey and demographic items, and c) we will fully debrief participants afterwards, including providing them the opportunity to decline to include their responses in the final data set.  
 
**Recruitment Methods:** 
 
We will recruit a convenience sample of participants. Study personnel will recruit people they know by word of mouth in person or via email, or by posting an invitation to participate on social media such as Facebook, Twitter, or other websites, including the Psychology Department’s SONA paid system website. The materials note that we’re recruiting adults ages 18 years and up who are currently in the United States and have not participated in this research previously. We will also recruit participants via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. Participants will earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of departmental course requirements. 
 
**Consent Process:**  
 
Participants will provide informed consent by reading the consent form online and then clicking a button in the Qualtrics survey.  
 
To ensure participant understanding of the study and its procedures, participants will have as much time as they would like to consider their participation. Should they have questions, the consent form will provide contact information for the PI. Participation will be dependent upon consent; participants will not be able to continue to the survey unless they have consented to participate. 
 
To minimize the possibility of coercion or undue influence, the consent form will make it clear that participation is voluntary and that potential participants may choose not to participate without penalty; similarly, the consent form will make it clear that participants may withdraw their participation without penalty too. In addition, researchers will not use unduly influential or coercive language in recruitment materials. 
 
 
**Compensation:**   
 
Some participants will have the opportunity to enter a drawing for $50. Participants who opt in and provide a valid email address in the contact information survey will be eligible. The drawing will take place after data collection is complete, likely on or near Wednesday, December 9, 2020. We will choose at least one winner. Compensation will be issued via Venmo or PayPal.  
 
Other participants will have the opportunity to earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of course requirements via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. 
 
The level of compensation is expected to be adequate to incentivize participation without being unduly influential. Participants who submit a survey but indicate they wish to exclude their data from analyses will still be eligible for compensation. 
 
There are no costs to participants. 
 
**Potential Benefits to Participants:**  
 
There are no direct benefits to participants beyond the educational experience of participating and the knowledge that they are contributing to our understanding of human psychology. 
 
**Risks to Participants:** 
 
The risks to participants are minimal. Procedures are largely limited to responding to survey questions about meat consumption and providing demographic information. These are common everyday experiences. For participants taking part in exchange for entering a drawing as compensation, there is also a slight risk of a breach of confidentiality because we are collecting identifiers (names, email addresses) from the participants who wish to enter the compensation drawing. However, the data we are collecting would not be considered sensitive by reasonable standards, thus the severity of a breach, in the unlikely event one were to occur, would be quite low in magnitude. See Data Management and Confidentiality, section, for the steps we will take to mitigate this risk.  
 
**Withdrawal of Participants:** 
 
We will not withdraw participants from the research without their consent.  
 
If participants withdraw by indicating they would like us to exclude their data from the final data set, we will delete their responses when the data are downloaded from Qualtrics, prior to analysis or sharing in a public web repository. We will not be able to delete responses from any participants who may contact the PI after-the-fact because survey data files will not enable us to identify their specific responses. 
 
**Data Management and Confidentiality:** 
 
All information will be collected via Qualtrics surveys that are housed in the PI’s password-protected account. The data collection survey will only house participant data without personal identifiers; the contact information survey will only house participant identifiers (name, email address) without data.  
 
To mitigate the risk of a breach of confidentiality, we will not maintain a link between identifiers and data. In addition, only individuals who have been approved as study personnel under this protocol will be given collaborative access to the surveys through their Tufts password-protected Qualtrics account on an as-needed basis. 
 
Once data collection is complete, the PI will download the data and contact information from the two surveys and store them on a password-protected Tufts computer. After verifying that the data are deidentified, she will make the data available in a public web repository for access by other researchers, including the student researchers in her PSY 32 course. The data will, thus, be stored indefinitely.  
 
As soon as the PI has completed the compensation drawing process, she will delete the contact information from the computer and from Qualtrics to further mitigate risk of a breach of confidentiality. 
 
**Provisions to Protect the Privacy and Confidentiality of Participants and the Research Data:** 
 
Participants will complete this study on a computer with internet access at a time and location of their choosing. We are not asking them to provide sensitive, personal information. Survey items are innocuous questions about meat consumption and demographics, but participants are free to decline to answer as they wish. In addition, our data management plan, as articulated above, is designed to minimize the risk of a breach of confidentiality. As such, participant privacy is well-protected.  
  
 
**Data Sharing:** 
 
The deidentified data will be shared in a public web repository (e.g., Open Science Framework, github, or other) for access by anyone with an internet connection indefinitely. Other researchers may use the data to contribute to a meta-analysis of direct replications of the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), and some may download the data to see if they can reproduce our results or generate novel insights in new analyses.

title_r: A Replication Study-Postoperative Complications in Bariatric Surgery using Age and BMI Stratification: A Stusy using ACS-NSQIP data (2014)
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the findings of Sanni et al.'s (2014) research on postoperative complications in bariatric surgery patients. The original research utilized age and BMI stratification and data from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS NSQIP) to identify the relationship between these variables and postoperative complications. The findings of the original study revealed significant associations between age, BMI, and postoperative complications. The replication plan aims to confirm these associations and identify the factors that lead to postoperative complications in patients undergoing bariatric surgery. The replication study proposes a comprehensive plan consisting of three types of analyses: pure replication, measurement and estimation analysis (MEA), and theory of change analysis (TCA). These analyses are designed to validate and expand on the discoveries of the original study. The pure replication phase is a critical step in the replication process, aiming to reproduce the original analyses accurately. This phase involves performing the statistical tests used in the original study to confirm the significant risk factors identified in the original study. Overall, the pure replication phase ensures the accuracy of the research findings. Conducting MEA (Measurement and Estimation Analysis) is crucial for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the findings. Employing alternative methods such as nonparametric tests will provide a more comprehensive analysis and help validate the results obtained in the pure replication phase. It is important to ensure that the conclusions drawn from the original study are robust and can be replicated using different statistical techniques. The concluding step, TCA (Theory of Change Analysis), will broaden the scope of the original study by examining the correlation between wound complications and diabetes status (YES/NO) among patients undergoing bariatric surgery. This analysis will employ Chi-Square tests and logistic regression 3 models to assess the association between diabetes and wound complications among patients undergoing bariatric surgery while accounting for variables including age and BMI. Through replicating the original study's findings and employing alternative analytical approaches, this research aims to enhance understanding of the determinants influencing postoperative complications among individuals undergoing bariatric surgery. Furthermore, by exploring novel inquiries concerning wound complications in patients with diabetes, this study aspires to inform the establishment of evidence driven protocols for bariatric surgery selection criteria, thereby fostering advancements in patient care and outcomes.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: Conceptual replication of Dignath et al., 2022, experiment 3 - particular focus on emotional Stroop task (E.g., Soutscheck and Schubert, 2013) 'Do self-related primes influence the processing of conflicts in the emotional domain?'
abstract_r: Previous research has shown (e.g., Dignath et al., 2022) that Congruency Effects (CE) in a gender Stroop task are significantly reduced when self-related primes are used compared neutral primes in a control condition. The significant interaction of the factors ‘congruency’ and ‘prime’, indicated reduced CEs in experimental blocks with self-referential information compared to control blocks. Here, we ask whether this phenomenon can be replicated also in the emotional domain. We will closely replicate experiment 3 of Dignath et al. (2022), but instead of a gender task, emotional Stroop task will be employed (modelled after Soutscheck & Schubert, 2013), in which participants must classify facial expressions as positive or negative, while ignoring clearly positive or negative valenced words. In line with the study of Dignath et al. (2022), the main question of this experiment is how self-referential primes modulate CEs. Going beyond previous research, we ask whether similar effects can be generalized to the emotional domain. We consider two possible accounts. The attentional bias account assumes that CEs should be increased in the self-referential condition, because self-referential primes draw attention towards the task-irrelevant dimension and hence should enhance CEs. Specifically, for emotional stimuli, it has been suggested that attention is not only quicker engaged by emotional stimuli, but also impairs attentional disengagement. In contrast, the priming of control account holds that CEs in the self-referential condition should be reduced, because self-relevance boosts cognitive control over task-irrelevant response tendencies. Indeed, it has been suggested that the inextricable link between control and self-referential information is particularly strong for emotional material.

title_r: Testing the Effects of Multiple Stigmas on Discrimination in the German Housing Market in political right and political liberal voting cities - a conceptual replication of Mazziotta, Zehr and Rohmann
abstract_r: Die Population umfasst private Vermieter*innen in sechs ausgewählten deutschen Städten, die basierend auf AfD-Wähleranteil bei der Europawahl 2024 klassifiziert werden. Die Städte Bielefeld (10,6%), Braunschweig (8,6%) und Aachen (10,8%) repräsentieren Regionen mit einem “niedrigen” AfD-Wähleranteil, während Chemnitz (28,2%), Magdeburg (22,0%) und Gelsenkirchen (27,7%) Regionen mit einen “hohen” AfD-Wähleranteil darstellen. Die Rekrutierung erfolgt indirekt durch das gezielte Senden standardisierter E-Mail- Anfragen über die Plattform Immoscout24 an private Vermieter*innen, die Immobilienanzeigen in den genannten Städten online geschaltet haben. Listings werden basierend auf vorher festgelegten Einschlusskriterien ausgewählt. Es wird eine Gleichverteilung zwischen den Bedingungen angestrebt, Jede Kombination von Nationalität, sexueller Orientierung und Städtetyp wird durch jeweils 75 Bewerbungen abgedeckt. Eingeschlossen werden Inserate, die die festgelegten Kriterien in Bezug auf Preis (maximal 1.000 Euro Warmmiete), Zimmeranzahl (2 bis 5 Zimmer), Wohnungsgröße (mindestens 50m2 und höchstens 200m2), Entfernung zum Stadtzentrum (maximal 20km) und Art des Vermieters (privat) erfüllen. Ausgeschlossen werden Inserate, die doppelt eingestellt wurden (Re-posts) oder seit länger als einem Monat online sind. Bei der Studie handelt es sich um ein Online-Feldexperiment, da reale Daten auf einer öffentlichen Plattform erhoben werden. Die Kontaktaufnahme erfolgt über ImmoScout24. Die Datenerhebung ist für den Zeitraum 28.11.2024 bis 15.01.2025 geplant. Sollten durch Ausschlusskriterien so viele Inserate ausgeschlossen werden, dass das angepeilte Power-Level von 0.95 nicht erreicht werden kann, erhöhen wir die Anzahl der Städte, in welchem wir erheben um die nächsthöchste und nächst niedrigste Stadt bezogen auf den AfD-Wähleranteil.

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic. This study is an exact replication study of a cross-sectional study. By using an online questionnaire and replicating the statistical analysis, we hope to answer the research questions of the original study: 1. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with the desire to be taller, 2. are characteristics of the dark triad associated with shorter height, and 3. are the correlations stronger in men than in women. For this purpose, we will recruit 616 participants through the study platform 'Prolific' to answer the following questionnaires and baseline information anonymously: 1. Dark Triad Dirty Dozen Questionnaire. 2. Height Dissatisfaction Subscale of the Male Body Attitudes Scale. 3. Demographic data. We will analyze the hypotheses using the same statistical methods as in the original study, i.e., Pearson correlation coefficient, Fischer Z-transformation, Steiger's Z-test, and multiple linear regressions.

title_r: Working memory capacity and the risky-choice framing effect: A preregistered replication and extension of Corbin et al. (2010)
abstract_r: Higher working memory capacity is associated with superior performance on a number of tasks but may it sometimes be paradoxically associated with suboptimal performance? Corbin et al. title_r: Replication Study of Infants’ Visual Cortical Connectivity and Later Autism
abstract_r: Backgrounds and Research Questions In an earlier study (Hardiansyah et al., 2025), we found that functional connectivity within 5-month-old infants’ visual cortex (VC) during viewing of social and non-social stimuli were predictive of their autism symptoms in toddlerhood. Specifically, we reported that connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area in theta band during non-social stimulus processing and in gamma band during social stimulus processing to be strong predictors (R2 > 50%) of later autism. Considering the potential importance of these findings in terms of identifying early markers of autism here we seek to replicate the results with an independent group of infants to provide further evidence in support of our earlier conclusions (Hardiansyah et al., 2025). Therefore, using data from the BASIS Network (https://www.basisnetwork.org) in the U.K., comprising eighty one 5-month-old infants representing both elevated autism likelihood and typical development groups, we plan to apply the same functional connectivity analyses (detailed in “Methods & Analysis” section) as used in our previous paper to address the following research questions: Hypothesis #1: Infants’ theta functional connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area during non-social stimulus processing is positively linked to their later autistic symptoms at 36 months. Hypothesis #2: Infants’ gamma functional connectivity between V1 and extrastriate area during social stimulus processing is positively linked to their later autistic symptoms at 36 months. In addition, we will assess whether the putative associations are moderated by familial likelihood status.

title_r: Prevalence-induced Concept Change in the Judgement of Male Bodies: A Replication and Extension of Devine et al. (2024)
abstract_r: The following study aims to replicate H1b from Devine et al. (2023). Here, the authors found that men were sensitive to prevalence-induced concept changes (PICC) when judging whether male bodies varying in muscularity were muscular or not, but not when judging whether male bodies varying in body fat were overweight or not. Furthermore, they found that men were overall faster in judging whether a body is muscular compared to judging whether a body is overweight. Taken together, these results lead the authors to suspect that men might have an attentional bias towards idealized male bodies, which manifests in faster and more selective extraction of muscle-related body information. Thus, Devine et al. show that PICC may not represent a general perceptual effect, but rather could be moderated by the specific stimulus category. Our main goal of the current study is to replicate the effect found that the strength of PICC in the judgment of male bodies depends on the specific stimulus category (weight-related, muscle-related). Furthermore, we intend to replicate the difference in response times between the judgments of these stimulus categories. The study design will be adjusted to control for possible confounding factors such as the order of the presented stimulus category. In addition, the stimulus material (computer-generated male bodies) will be adapted in order to achieve better comparability between the stimulus categories. Furthermore, we will examine whether the degree of body dissatisfaction (BD) related to different body characteristics (weight-related, muscle-related) influences whether participants judge muscle-related bodies faster than weight-related bodies, or vice versa. Recent studies suggest that attentional biases toward body-related stimuli specifically affect men with higher BD rather than the general population, and that the impact might differ depending on whether men experience more muscle-related or weight-related BD (Joseph et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2018; Porras-Garcia et al., 2020; Talbot & Saleme, 2022; Kirby et al., 2023). Therefore, BD will be measured separately for both stimulus categories (weight-related, muscle-related) (Ralph-Nearman & Filik, 2018).

title_r: A replication and extension of “Task difficulty modulates the disrupting effects of oral respiration on visual search performance” (Yoshimura et al. 2019)
abstract_r: The relationship between breathing and cognition is gaining increasing interest, with nasal breathing linked to greater neurophysiological synchrony compared to oral breathing. This synchrony could impact cognitive functions like attention and memory. Yoshimura et al. (2019) examined whether respiratory pathway (oral vs. nasal) affects visual search performance. In their second experiment, oral breathing combined with reduced target discriminability led to increased reaction time (RT) intercepts compared to nasal breathing, but only in the most difficult search condition. In this pre-registered report, we aim to replicate their RT effects and provide a more sensitive test of respiration effects by examining search efficiency across a wider range of difficulties. Using a within-subjects design, participants will complete a visual search task under oral and nasal breathing conditions, with target-distractor orientation differences ranging from 2° to 6°. This will show whether oral breathing speeds RT under difficult conditions (replicating Yoshimura et al.) and reduces search slopes (extending their findings). By examining both intercept and slope effects, we seek to determine whether oral breathing disrupts pre-search or post-search processing and/or impairs search efficiency. This research contributes to understanding how breathing pathway influences attentional processing during visual search tasks.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 3 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

People often find bullet points easier to understand than prose and generally prefer simpler explanations over complex ones. This preference reflects Occam’s razor—the idea that unnecessary assumptions should be avoided—and is considered an “explanatory virtue.” Some argue that simple explanations are more likely to be true, though probability alone may not fully explain the phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022).

Sehl et al. (2024) propose that the preference for simplicity reflects a broader tendency to favor efficiency in goal-directed activities. Explanation is one such activity: understanding an outcome is more efficient when fewer causes or assumptions are invoked. From this “efficiency” perspective, the preference for simplicity should appear not only in explanatory judgments (why an outcome occurred) but also in process judgments (how an outcome could be achieved). The theory further predicts that statistical information about reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates, likelihoods) can reduce or even reverse the simplicity preference. Seven preregistered experiments supported these predictions.

Because prior participants were mostly from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), questions remain about the universality of these findings. The present study replicates Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), testing the claim that preferences for simpler explanations reflect pursuit of efficiency. By using Japanese participants, we examine cross-cultural generality, extend the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on cultural variation in cognition.

This study (Study 3 of the project) focuses on replicating Sehl et al.’s Study 7. Their findings indicated that when a complex cause was more probable, the preference for the simple explanation diminished, particularly in process judgments.

In Study 7 of the previous work, participants more often chose the simple cause in explanatory than in process judgments. They also showed stronger preference for the simple cause when likelihoods were 80% vs. 65% than when they were 90% vs. 65%. Although the interaction was not statistically significant, a single-sample test revealed that only in the process-judgment condition with 90% vs. 65% likelihoods was the complex cause chosen significantly more often.

Judgments overall were shaped more by perceived probability of success (that an explanation was true or a process would succeed) than by ease of comprehension or number of factors. Probability information had greater weight in process judgments, whereas number of factors mattered more in explanatory choices.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 1 and 2 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

People often find information presented in bullet points easier to understand than lengthy prose, and in general prefer simpler explanations over more complex ones. This preference aligns with the principle of Occam’s razor, which holds that unnecessary assumptions should not be introduced, and has been regarded as one of the “explanatory virtues” used to evaluate the quality of explanations. Some have argued that simple explanations are more likely to be true than complex ones. However, it has also been suggested that probability alone cannot fully account for this phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022).

Sehl et al. (2024) propose a novel theory that the preference for simplicity is not unique to explanation itself, but rather stems from a broader tendency to favor efficient means of achieving goals. Providing an explanation is a goal-directed activity aimed at understanding the causes of an outcome, and from this perspective, explanations with fewer causes and assumptions can be seen as more efficient. According to this “doing things efficiently” account, the preference for simpler causes should manifest not only when judging why an outcome occurred (explanatory judgments), but also when evaluating how an outcome could be achieved (process judgments). Moreover, the theory predicts that when statistical information about the reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates or likelihood of effect occurrence) is provided, the preference for simplicity may weaken or even reverse. Sehl et al. support these predictions with evidence from seven preregistered experiments.

However, participants in prior studies were recruited primarily from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), leaving open questions about the universality of these findings. title_r: Replication Study: Feeling capable and valued
abstract_r: This study is a preregistered replication-with-extension of Bacq and Alt (2018), who examined how empathy influences social entrepreneurial (SE) intentions via two mechanisms: SE self-efficacy (agentic pathway) and social worth (communal pathway). Their original two-wave study with SE students showed that empathic concern and perspective-taking strengthened SE self-efficacy and social worth, which in turn enhanced SE intentions. We replicate this core model using the same constructs and theoretical framework to ensure comparability, with three key modifications. First, the study employs a single-wave survey design rather than the original two-wave structure to improve feasibility and reduce participant attrition; procedural and statistical remedies (e.g., anonymity and marker-variable checks) will mitigate potential common-method bias. Second, the measure of social worth has been adapted to allow broader applicability beyond project-based SE courses. The original wording (“the people I helped”) was course-specific, so the revised items assess the general sense of being valued, appreciated, and trusted by others for one’s contributions, aligning with the conceptual definition of social worth as feeling needed, cared about, and valued by others. Third, the empathy scales for perspective-taking and empathic concern are measured on 7-point scales instead of the original 5-point scales to harmonize all predictor constructs, increase response granularity, and enhance comparability. Our extension also introduces a broader student sample that includes both SE-course students and non-SE students. This design addresses potential selection bias inherent in studying only SE students, who may already be predisposed toward social impact careers. By including non-SE students, the study tests whether the proposed mechanisms operate consistently across both groups. If the mechanisms are correct, they should explain variation in SE intentions across groups, not just high levels among SE students. The outcomes will contribute to (social) entrepreneurship research by (a) reinforcing confidence in prior findings, (b) addressing potential selection bias in SE education research, and (c) clarifying the extent to which empathy-driven mechanisms explain differences in SE intentions across student populations.

title_r: Strengthening Democracy with interventions: A conceptual replication of a megastudy in the Netherlands
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Voelkel et al. 2024 published an intervention tournament aimed at testing interventions to reduce affective polarization, support for undemocratic practices and support for political violence in the United States. We will conduct a conceptual replication of this intervention tournament in the Netherlands. We will include five interventions from Voelkel et al. 2024, and, where necessary, adapt them to the different national context. We will also include three existing interventions that are already in use in the Netherlands, but to our knowledge, have not been evaluated. We also developed five new interventions that will be tested in the study. We adapted the dependent variables of the study to the national context while also refining their operationalization to improve instrument quality. We will test our interventions using a random sample of 22,500 Dutch citizens from the general adult population in the winter of 2026.

title_r: Breathing Route Does Not Affect Visual Search: A Pre-Registered Replication and Extension
abstract_r: The relationship between breathing and cognition is gaining increasing interest, with nasal breathing linked to greater neurophysiological synchrony compared to oral breathing. This synchrony could impact cognitive functions like attention and memory. Yoshimura et al. (2019) examined whether respiratory pathway (oral vs. nasal) affects visual search performance. In their second experiment, oral breathing combined with reduced target discriminability led to increased reaction time (RT) intercepts compared to nasal breathing, but only in the most difficult search condition. In this pre-registered report, we aim to replicate their RT effects and provide a more sensitive test of respiration effects by examining search efficiency across a wider range of difficulties. Using a within-subjects design, participants will complete a visual search task under oral and nasal breathing conditions, with target-distractor orientation differences ranging from 2° to 6°. This will show whether oral breathing speeds RT under difficult conditions (replicating Yoshimura et al.) and reduces search slopes (extending their findings). By examining both intercept and slope effects, we seek to determine whether oral breathing disrupts pre-search or post-search processing and/or impairs search efficiency. This research contributes to understanding how breathing pathway influences attentional processing during visual search tasks.

title_r: A Replication Study of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-Induced Heart-Brain Coupling
abstract_r: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is a prominent stimulation target for the treatment of Major Depressive disorder (MDD) with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). The therapeutic effect of DLPFC stimulation likely stems from the DLPFC–subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) connectivity. A recent study suggested that there is an overlap of the hubs in the depression network, including the DLPFC, sgACC, and vagus nerve (VN), with the heart-brain axis, and that stimulation of these hubs consequently leads to heart rate (HR) decelerations. A specific 10 Hz Dash rTMS protocol (‘neuro-cardiac guided rTMS version 2.0’, NGC-2.0 rTMS) has been proposed to induce coupling of TMS and HR changes (heart-brain coupling; HBC). This research encompasses two studies aimed at exploring the effects of NGC-TMS targeting the DLPFC. In the Study-1, we will replicate and corroborate previous findings with a larger cohort of twenty healthy young participants. These participants will undergo NGC-TMS sessions targeting the DLPFC, supplemented by sham TMS, across three sessions. Following these findings, the Study-2 will examine the robustness of HBC by assessing various stimulation intensities by targeting the most effective target identified in the Study-1.

title_r: A Replication Study of "Business as Plan B: Institutional foundations of gender inequality in entrepreneurship across 24 industrialized countries."
abstract_r: This study conducts a hybrid replication of Thébaud's (2015) investigation of institutional foundations of gender inequality in entrepreneurship across 24 industrialized countries. We combine exact replication—by designing our own survey instrument following the original methodology—with constructive replication by extending the sample to include non-industrialized countries. This extension tests the generalizability of Thébaud's institutional explanations beyond industrialized contexts and addresses a significant scope limitation in the original work. While the original study analyzed Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) data from 2001-2008, our contemporary data collection necessarily reflects current conditions, which allows us to assess whether the institutional mechanisms identified by Thébaud remain operative in today's entrepreneurial landscape. Our custom survey design reduces measurement error and provides better control over data quality compared to secondary data sources. We document all methodological differences from the original study, conduct power analyses to ensure adequate statistical confidence, and perform cross-country adjustments to address potential threats to validity arising from sample heterogeneity between industrialized and non-industrialized settings. This replication adds scientific value by simultaneously testing the robustness and temporal stability of influential findings while examining boundary conditions and alternative mechanisms in diverse economic contexts.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Rilliard & Moraes (2017) on Attitudinal Prosody in Brazilian Portuguese
abstract_r: Este Relato Registrado (Stage 1) apresenta uma replicação e extensão do estudo de Rilliard e Moraes (2017) sobre prosódia atitudinal no português brasileiro. O objetivo é investigar os correlatos perceptivos e acústicos de significados atitudinais socialmente relevantes expressos na fala em contextos comunicativos face a face. Com base no delineamento original, o protocolo introduz um conjunto controlado de estímulos visuais sintéticos para aumentar a padronização contextual e a replicabilidade experimental. O estudo compreende duas fases: uma tarefa de produção, em que falantes produzem enunciados sob cenários atitudinais induzidos visualmente, e uma tarefa de percepção, na qual ouvintes avaliam os significados pretendidos. As medidas acústicas incluem frequência fundamental (F0), intensidade, duração e parâmetros espectrais, extraídos no Praat e analisados em R e Python. As hipóteses, o plano amostral, os critérios de exclusão e as análises estatísticas estão especificados a priori. Todos os materiais e scripts serão disponibilizados em repositório público. O estudo busca contribuir para a reprodutibilidade da pesquisa em prosódia atitudinal e para o refinamento metodológico de investigações experimentais sobre entoação socialmente indexada no português brasileiro.

title_r: Unfinished Tasks and Rumination: A Replication Study on the Mediating Role of Competence Need Satisfaction and the Moderating Effects of Proactive Work Behavior and Leisure Crafting
abstract_r: Work-related rumination (WRR) defines a state of perseverative cognitive activation in which work continues to occupy the employee's mind during off-job hours (Querstret & Cropley, 2012). Research distinguishes between three components: problem pondering, detachment, and affective rumination. Among these, only affective rumination has a negative valence, while problem pondering is positive and detachment is neutral. A growing body of literature indicates that unfinished tasks link most strongly to affective rumination (Wendsche et al., 2026), with recent research suggesting that competence need satisfaction mediates the relationship and proactive work behavior moderates it (Weigelt et al., 2019). To extend prior work, this study will examine leisure crafting, contributing to the understanding of potential moderators under which the relationship between unfinished tasks and affective rumination holds, thereby providing opportunities for intervention research.
